entries.content:
MCP bridges the gap between your AI agents and your external tools, allowing them to send Discord messages, read your emails, and interact with your environment. But this massive leap in capability comes with a serious catch: massive security risks.

Because anyone can build and open-source an MCP server, integrating them blindly can lead to devastating breaches. To help you navigate this new landscape, we just published the MCP Security Fundamentals Course on the freeCodeCamp.org YouTube channel.

This comprehensive 2-hour course will get you up to speed on what MCP is, the risks it introduces, and exactly how to use it securely.

In this course, you will learn:

  • The Basics of MCP

    What it is, how it works, and why it is transforming AI applications.
  • Real-World Breaches

    A breakdown of "Patient Zero" MCP exploits and how seemingly harmless community tools can be weaponized.
  • The OWASP MCP Top 10

    A deep dive into the biggest vulnerabilities in the MCP ecosystem and how to mitigate them.
  • Building an MCP Security Program

    The five pillars of enterprise defense, including discovery, governance, identity and access, defense in depth, and detection.
  • Compliance & Governance

    How to navigate frameworks like the EU AI Act, NIST AI RMF, and ISO 42001.

Watch the full course on the freeCodeCamp.org YouTube channel (2-hour watch).

entries.content:
Over time, knowledge has been passed down in various forms. Before writing was invented in ancient Mesopotamia (modern-day Iraq), laws, history, myths, songs, and other information were all transferred from generation to generation orally. This was done either via instructions or storytelling (especially folktales and events that had happened over time).

But another common method of knowledge transfer is from teacher to student, whether formally or informally. We’ve seen this throughout time as well: the Bible recorded that Jesus had twelve disciples whom he taught daily from the start of his mission to his death. Socrates taught Plato. Plato went on to establish an academy in Athens, where he taught Aristotle for twenty years. Aristotle revolutionized science, logic, and politics. And the list goes on.

A 21st-century example of this is deep learning AI lineage. During the 20th-century AI winter, when we thought neural networks were a dead end, this teacher-student lineage kept the dream alive.

Geoffrey Hinton, regarded as the father of AI, ran a lab where he taught Yann LeCun, Ilya Sutskever, and others. Yann LeCun went on to invent the convolutional neural network (CNN), while Ilya Sutskever co-founded OpenAI before leaving for Safe Superintelligence Inc.

While the concept of knowledge transfer between humans is quite familiar, how about knowledge transfer from machine to machine? This is known as "model distillation."

In this article, I'm going to break down what model distillation is. We'll explore the techniques it uses, and I'll walk you through how to implement it from scratch using PyTorch.

By the end, you'll understand how to train smaller, more efficient models and how distillation compares to other compression techniques like quantization and pruning.

What We'll Cover

Prerequisites

To follow along, you should have the following:

  • A GitHub Repository: The complete implementation of the project is available here, and you should clone it to follow along.

  • Basic familiarity with Python and object-oriented programming concepts (for example, working with classes).

  • An overview of deep learning fundamentals. You should understand concepts like epochs, forward propagation, loss function, and so on.

  • PyTorch Basics: While I'll explain each code section for you, basic familiarity with PyTorch tensors and training loops will be helpful.

  • A development environment: You should have Python installed on your machine. I'll be using Visual Studio Code as my editor, but you can use any editor or IDE of your choice.

  • Hardware: For this project, we'll be using a relatively small dataset so a standard CPU will work well.

What is Model Distillation?

Model distillation (or knowledge distillation) is an approach that aims to pass on the learned behavior of a large, highly accurate model to a smaller, computationally efficient model that's better suited for practical deployment.

Distillation is a compression technique where a smaller model (known as the student) learns to mimic the output of a larger, more complex model (the teacher). The goal is for the student model to achieve a level of performance close to the teacher, but with significantly fewer parameters, making it more efficient for deployment. (Source)

Why is Model Distillation Necessary?

At the time of this writing, both closed-source and open-source models are trained on trillions of parameters. These are the internal configuration variables that models learn automatically from training data. This immense number of parameters makes it extremely difficult and expensive to run without proper funding. Models consume large amounts of energy and require expensive hardware.

With distillation, we can transfer the learnings of these frontier models to smaller, more efficient models, making them easier and cheaper to use.

Model Distillation Techniques

The distillation technique used depends on the knowledge that's being transferred. Some methods transfer only the final prediction. Others transfer internal representation, attention maps, reasoning steps, or even the entire behavior of the teacher model.

These are some of the techniques:

Response-Based Distillation

Originally introduced by Geoffrey Hinton in his paper Distilling the knowledge in a neural network, this is the classic teacher-to-student distillation. Before diving deep into how it works, there are a few concepts you need to understand about model training: hard labels and soft labels.

Hard labels deal strictly with fixed categorical targets. When a picture of a dog is fed into a model and it's asked to predict if it's a dog, cat, or horse, it predicts it's a dog, given the result as Dog(1), horse(0), and cat(0). There's no probability as to what percentage or features of the picture look like a cat or a horse.

But we also have soft labels, which deal with probability. When the same picture is fed to a model using soft labels, it can predict that the picture has a 0.85 probability of being a dog, a 0.10 probability of being a cat, and a 0.5 probability of being a horse.

In response-based distillation, instead of training the student model with hard labels, it also learns from the probability of the teacher model's output (soft labels). The student can learn that the picture is a dog, but it also learns that the picture also slightly resembles a cat and barely resembles a horse.

This additional information is called dark knowledge. It enables the smaller model to copy the behavior of a larger, more accurate teacher while maintaining high performance.

Some of the advantages of response-based distillation are that it's easy to implement, it's very stable, and it works well with image classification. But there are some drawbacks, the major one being that it ignores what happens inside the network.

That is, response base distillation only looks at the output layer (the probabilities), so the student has a "black-box" relationship with the teacher model. It learns what the teacher decides, but not how it comes to that conclusion. Using the previous example, it learns the probability of what feature is a dog, cat and horse but not the underlying principle or workings of how that conclusion was made.

Feature-Based Distillation

This technique transfers the internal feature representation of the larger model rather than transferring only the final output.

An easy way to think about this is to imagine that you're a student of a great math tutor. The tutor gives you a math problem and shows you their final result. You might eventually guess the right formula, but you're mostly just learning to memorize output.

But if the tutor requires you to look at their notebook and see their work, you're learning the tutor's exact thought process.

In feature-based distillation, during training, the student model is required to produce hidden layer activations that match those of the tutor using Mean Squared Error (MSE). With mean squared error, the student model isn't just rewarded for correctly guessing the final output. It's also penalised if its internal function system doesn't match that of the teacher model.

This method is heavily used in convolutional neural networks, vision transformers, object detection, and so on.

The drawbacks of this method are that since the student has to extract and store internal feature map of the teacher model at every training iteration, memory and power consumption can quickly escalate. This makes it very expensive to run.

Attention Distillation

In this approach, instead of the student model copying all the neurons, it observes where the larger model pays attention and copies those neurons.

In transformer models, which are models that try to make sense of a sentence instead of paying attention to individual words, attention maps indicate which input tokens or regions the model considers most important when making predictions. The student tries to reproduce those maps or the distribution of the teacher model. This shows the student where to "look" when trying to solve a problem.

The drawback of attention distillation is substantial overhead in both training time and hardware resource. This is because metrics like Mean Squared Error (MSE) and Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence need to be calculated. These metrics act as a loss function that tells a model exactly how much it's prediction or internal representation differs from the teacher model. Making this calculation across massive attention tensors contribute significantly to resource consumption.

Self-Distillation

A model is also capable of training itself. This involves knowledge transfer from an earlier version to a later version. It can also involve the transfer of knowledge between different layers in the network.

An advantage of this is that the model can become better without necessarily growing in size, reducing the cost of using a larger model to train the student model.

How to Implement Knowledge Distillation in PyTorch.

To showcase how model distillation works in real time, we'll be training a teacher and then a student model using the MNIST dataset and classifier with PyTorch.

The dataset contains about 70,000 greyscale images of handwritten digits. We'll train the teacher, then freeze it while we train a student using hard labels and soft targets from the teacher.

Note that the MNIST dataset is a relatively small dataset, so our distillation gains might not be much. But this project showcases the distillation workflow, and it will give you a good background to run larger datasets.

To run this project, you'll need the following Python packages:

PackagePurpose
torch
 The core deep learning framework we'll use to build and train neural networks.
torchvision
 Provides datasets like MNIST and image utilities.
numpy
 Numerical computations and array operations.
matplotlib
 Plotting graphs and visualizing the visual images/results.
tqdm
 Displays progress bars during training.

For this project, I'll be working with the Visual Studio Code editor, but you can use any other code editor of your choice.

This is our project structure. I'll be explaining the folders and files below alongside the code for our project.

│
├── data/
│
├── models.py
│
├── engine.py
│
├── losses.py
│
├── train_teacher.py
│
├── train_student.py

First in our folder structure is our 

data
folder. This contains our MNIST dataset.

Our 

models.py
file defines the architecture of every neural network used in the project. It contains the teacher network class and student network class. Each class defines layers, forward propagation, and how data flow through the network.
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

class TeacherNet(nn.Module):

    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()

        self.flatten = nn.Flatten()

        self.fc1 = nn.Linear(28 * 28, 1024)
        self.fc2 = nn.Linear(1024, 512)
        self.fc3 = nn.Linear(512, 256)
        self.fc4 = nn.Linear(256, 128)
        self.fc5 = nn.Linear(128, 10)

    def forward(self, x):

        x = self.flatten(x)

        x = F.relu(self.fc1(x))
        x = F.relu(self.fc2(x))
        x = F.relu(self.fc3(x))
        x = F.relu(self.fc4(x))

        logits = self.fc5(x)

        return logits


class StudentNet(nn.Module):
    """
    Smaller neural network (Student)
    """

    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()

        self.flatten = nn.Flatten()

        self.fc1 = nn.Linear(28 * 28, 128)
        self.fc2 = nn.Linear(128, 10)

    def forward(self, x):

        x = self.flatten(x)

        x = F.relu(self.fc1(x))

        logits = self.fc2(x)

        return logits

The 

utils.py
file prepares the dataset and answers the question, "Where does the dataset come from?" Here, we download the MNIST dataset, normalize the images, and create our training and testing loader.
from torchvision import datasets, transforms
from torch.utils.data import DataLoader


def get_dataloaders(batch_size=64):
    """
    Downloads MNIST (if needed) and returns
    training and testing DataLoaders.
    """

    transform = transforms.ToTensor()

    train_dataset = datasets.MNIST(
        root="data",
        train=True,
        download=True,
        transform=transform
    )

    test_dataset = datasets.MNIST(
        root="data",
        train=False,
        download=True,
        transform=transform
    )

    train_loader = DataLoader(
        train_dataset,
        batch_size=batch_size,
        shuffle=True
    )

    test_loader = DataLoader(
        test_dataset,
        batch_size=batch_size,
        shuffle=False
    )

    return train_loader, test_loader

The 

engine.py
file contains the reusable learning algorithm and helps with how training happens. It receives the model.py code and trains it.
import torch
from tqdm import tqdm


def train_one_epoch(
    model,
    dataloader,
    criterion,
    optimizer,
    device,
):
    model.train()

    running_loss = 0

    progress = tqdm(dataloader)

    for images, labels in progress:

        images = images.to(device)
        labels = labels.to(device)

        optimizer.zero_grad()

        outputs = model(images)

        loss = criterion(outputs, labels)

        loss.backward()

        optimizer.step()

        running_loss += loss.item()

        progress.set_description(
            f"Loss {loss.item():.4f}"
        )

    return running_loss / len(dataloader)


def evaluate(model, dataloader, device):

    model.eval()

    correct = 0
    total = 0

    with torch.no_grad():

        for images, labels in dataloader:

            images = images.to(device)
            labels = labels.to(device)

            outputs = model(images)

            _, predicted = torch.max(outputs, dim=1)

            total += labels.size(0)

            correct += (predicted == labels).sum().item()

    accuracy = 100 * correct / total

    return accuracy


def predict(model, images, device):

    model.eval()

    with torch.no_grad():

        images = images.to(device)

        outputs = model(images)

        _, predictions = torch.max(outputs, dim=1)

    return predictions

def train_distillation_epoch(
    teacher,
    student,
    dataloader,
    optimizer,
    device,
    loss_fn,
    temperature=4.0,
    alpha=0.5,
):
    """
    Train the student using a frozen teacher.
    """

    teacher.eval()
    student.train()

    running_loss = 0

    progress = tqdm(dataloader)

    for images, labels in progress:

        images = images.to(device)
        labels = labels.to(device)

        optimizer.zero_grad()

        # Teacher predictions (NO gradients)
        with torch.no_grad():
            teacher_logits = teacher(images)

        # Student predictions
        student_logits = student(images)

        # Combined loss
        loss = loss_fn(
            student_logits=student_logits,
            teacher_logits=teacher_logits,
            labels=labels,
            temperature=temperature,
            alpha=alpha,
        )

        loss.backward()

        optimizer.step()

        running_loss += loss.item()

        progress.set_description(
            f"Distill Loss {loss.item():.4f}"
        )

    return running_loss / len(dataloader)

The 

losses.py
file defines how the model measures its mistake. Since a neural network learns by minimizing loss, for baseline visualize used 
CrossEntropyLoss
, and for knowledge distillation, we introduced 
distillation_loss()
.

Inside this file, we combined hard labels and soft targets using cross entropy and k1 divergence. This is where Geoffrey Hinton's algorithm lives.

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

cross_entropy = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()


def distillation_loss(
    student_logits,
    teacher_logits,
    labels,
    temperature=4.0,
    alpha=0.5,
):
    """
    Geoffrey Hinton's Knowledge Distillation Loss

    Parameters
    ----------
    student_logits : output from student model
    teacher_logits : output from teacher model
    labels         : ground-truth labels
    temperature    : controls softness of probability distribution
    alpha          : weight between hard and soft losses
    """

    # Hard Label Loss
    hard_loss = cross_entropy(student_logits, labels)

    # Teacher Soft Targets
    teacher_probs = F.softmax(
        teacher_logits / temperature,
        dim=1
    )

    # Student Soft Predictions
    student_log_probs = F.log_softmax(
        student_logits / temperature,
        dim=1
    )

    # KL Divergence
    soft_loss = F.kl_div(
        student_log_probs,
        teacher_probs,
        reduction="batchmean"
    )

    # Final Distillation Loss
    loss = (
        alpha * hard_loss
        +
        (1 - alpha)
        * (temperature ** 2)
        * soft_loss
    )

    return loss

The 

train_teacher.py
file is to train the teacher network. After running this for the first time, we don't train the teacher again.
import torch
import torch.optim as optim

from models import TeacherNet
from utils import get_dataloaders
from engine import train_one_epoch, evaluate
from losses import cross_entropy

device = torch.device(
    "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"
)

train_loader, test_loader = get_dataloaders()

teacher = TeacherNet().to(device)

optimizer = optim.Adam(
    teacher.parameters(),
    lr=0.001,
)

epochs = 10

for epoch in range(epochs):

    loss = train_one_epoch(
        teacher,
        train_loader,
        cross_entropy,
        optimizer,
        device,
    )

    accuracy = evaluate(
        teacher,
        test_loader,
        device,
    )

    print(
        f"Epoch {epoch+1}/{epochs}"
        f" | Loss: {loss:.4f}"
        f" | Accuracy: {accuracy:.2f}%"
    )

torch.save(
    teacher.state_dict(),
    "teacher.pth",
)

print("\nTeacher saved successfully.")

The 

train_student.p
y file is where we train the student. It's identical to that of the train_teacher except it's a smaller network and no teacher guidance is implemented here. This gives the baseline accuracy of how the student will perform without the teacher.
import torch
import torch.optim as optim

from models import StudentNet
from utils import get_dataloaders
from engine import train_one_epoch, evaluate
from losses import cross_entropy

device = torch.device(
    "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"
)

train_loader, test_loader = get_dataloaders()

student = StudentNet().to(device)

optimizer = optim.Adam(
    student.parameters(),
    lr=0.001,
)

epochs = 10

for epoch in range(epochs):

    loss = train_one_epoch(
        student,
        train_loader,
        cross_entropy,
        optimizer,
        device,
    )

    accuracy = evaluate(
        student,
        test_loader,
        device,
    )

    print(
        f"Epoch {epoch+1}/{epochs}"
        f" | Loss: {loss:.4f}"
        f" | Accuracy: {accuracy:.2f}%"
    )

torch.save(
    student.state_dict(),
    "student_baseline.pth",
)

print("\nBaseline student saved.")

The 

train_distilled_student.py
is the heart of this code. In this file, we teach the student using both labels and the teacher's knowledge. Here, we implement response-based knowledge distillation.
import torch
import torch.optim as optim

from models import TeacherNet, StudentNet
from utils import get_dataloaders
from engine import (
    train_distillation_epoch,
    evaluate,
)
from losses import distillation_loss

device = torch.device(
    "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"
)

train_loader, test_loader = get_dataloaders()

# Load Teacher
teacher = TeacherNet().to(device)
teacher.load_state_dict(
    torch.load(
        "teacher.pth",
        map_location=device,
    )
)

teacher.eval()

# Student
student = StudentNet().to(device)

optimizer = optim.Adam(
    student.parameters(),
    lr=0.001,
)

epochs = 10

for epoch in range(epochs):

    loss = train_distillation_epoch(
        teacher,
        student,
        train_loader,
        optimizer,
        device,
        distillation_loss,
        temperature=3,
        alpha=0.7,
    )

    accuracy = evaluate(
        student,
        test_loader,
        device,
    )

    print(
        f"Epoch {epoch+1}/{epochs}"
        f" | Loss: {loss:.4f}"
        f" | Accuracy: {accuracy:.2f}%"
    )

torch.save(
    student.state_dict(),
    "student_distilled.pth",
)

print("\nDistilled student saved.")

The 

evaluate.py
measures how well a trained model performs. Here, we simply load the model, load test data, predict, and compute the accuracy.
import torch

from models import TeacherNet
from utils import get_dataloaders
from engine import evaluate

device = torch.device(
    "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"
)

_, test_loader = get_dataloaders()

teacher = TeacherNet().to(device)

teacher.load_state_dict(
    torch.load(
        "teacher.pth",
        map_location=device,
    )
)

accuracy = evaluate(
    teacher,
    test_loader,
    device,
)

print(
    f"Teacher Accuracy: {accuracy:.2f}%"
)

The 

visualize.py
file is to present our findings visually. We use the Python package matplotlib to visualise the results of our teacher, baseline student, and distilled student.
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

models = [
    "Teacher",
    "Baseline\nStudent",
    "Distilled\nStudent"
]

accuracy = [98.20, 97.86, 97.91]

plt.figure(figsize=(7,5))
plt.bar(models, accuracy)

plt.title("Knowledge Distillation Performance Comparison")
plt.ylabel("Accuracy (%)")

for i, v in enumerate(accuracy):
    plt.text(i, v + 0.02, f"{v:.2f}%", ha="center")

plt.ylim(97.5, 98.5)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig("accuracy_comparison.png", dpi=300)
plt.show()

You can see the entire workflow of our program below so you understand how everything comes together:

                       utils.py
                          │
                 Load MNIST Dataset
                          │
                          ▼
                     models.py
             TeacherNet / StudentNet
                          │
                          ▼
                     losses.py
  Cross Entropy + Distillation Loss Function
                          │
                          ▼
                     engine.py
    Generic Training and Evaluation Functions
             ┌────────────┼────────────┐
             │            │            │
             ▼            ▼            ▼
  train_teacher.py  train_student.py  distilled_student.py
             │            │            │
             ▼            ▼            ▼
   teacher.pth  student_baseline.pth  distilled.pth
                          │
                          ▼
                     evaluate.py
              Compute Final Accuracy
                          │
                          ▼
                    visualize.py
     Generate Charts and Experimental Figures

How to Evaluate the Results

Now, let's check and evaluate our results. These are screenshots from running ten epochs for each of the networks: the teacher, student, and distilled student network.

Teacher Network: After 10 complete cycles, we attained an accuracy of 98.20%.

Student Network: After 10 complete cycles, we attained an accuracy of 97.74%. This is a pretty good performance for a smaller network without the teacher model.

Distilled Student Network: After 10 complete cycle, we attained an accuracy of 98.20%. We had an improvement from 97.74% achieved without the teacher's model knowledge.

Other Approaches for Reducing Model Size

Now that we've seen what model distillation is with real-world code examples. Let's look at other approaches that developers are taking to reduce the size of large language models to save on latency, memory footprints, and compute cost and how they differ from distillation.

We have three other major approaches for this:

Quantization

Quantization achieves efficiency by strictly reducing the bit-width of the underlying data types used to store numerical weight and activations of the neural network. It targets the memory bandwidth bottleneck rather than the model architecture.

In simple terms, quantization can change a 32-bit number to 8-bit numbers, which saves about 75% of the file size.

A real-world example of how quantization differs from distillation is trying to save resources like ink and paper when printing a textbook. Distillation summarizes the textbook, while quantization prints the exact thing but uses a lower-resolution font to save ink and paper.

Pruning

Pruning operates on the principle that large language models often have too many redundant and low-impact parameters on the network. By removing weak connections, models can become smaller and faster.

For the textbook analogy, the pruning process is like going through the textbook and ripping off pages or chapters that you feel aren't needed.

Low-Rank Factorization

This is a mathematical process that uses linear algebra to simplify the matrix multiplication that dominates the deep learning architecture.

With the textbook example, this process involves rewriting complex sentences into simpler, shorter formulas that mean the same thing.

Choosing which method to use depends on the bottleneck you're trying to solve. Quantization generally works well for memory challenges, while pruning and distillation are designed to reduce computation time.

Conclusion

Knowledge transfer is as fundamental to artificial intelligence as it is to human history. Just as Aristotle built upon the teachings of Plato, today's efficient, deployable neural networks rely on the foundational "dark knowledge" extracted from massive, compute-heavy teacher models.

While training trillion-parameter frontier models requires immense hardware and financial resources, knowledge distillation ensures that the practical benefits of these advancements aren't locked behind massive computational bottlenecks.

As we demonstrated with the PyTorch MNIST experiment, even a simple response-based distillation can help a smaller network punch above its weight class by learning from the soft probabilities of a larger teacher.

When combined with other optimization techniques like quantization and pruning, distillation provides a clear pathway for deploying highly capable AI on edge devices, mobile phones, and consumer-grade hardware.

Thank you for reading! Please check out my YouTube channel, where I post videos on AI-related content.

entries.title: How to Diagnose vite: not found After npm ci in a Container Build
entries.summary: I recently worked on a project where a Node.js application used Vite to compile its frontend. It worked in a browser-hosted development environment, but its image build failed after the move to Azure
entries.content:
I recently worked on a project where a Node.js application used Vite to compile its frontend. It worked in a browser-hosted development environment, but its image build failed after the move to Azure Container Registry. The build reported a missing Vite executable after an earlier dependency install had failed.

The container build ended with a simple error:

sh: 1: vite: not found

Vite already appeared in 

devDependencies
. The build stage had run 
npm ci
before calling the build script. The Dockerfile looked ordinary, so the first explanations all pointed at dependency selection or 
NODE_ENV
.

The missing binary came from an earlier failure. 

npm ci
had tried to download hundreds of tarballs from a package host that only existed inside the browser-based development environment. It printed 
Exit handler never called!
, left 
node_modules
empty, and didn't give Docker a clear failure status. The following layer reached 
npm run build
and reported the first missing executable it needed.

The lockfile pointed npm at an unreachable host. This tutorial shows how to check whether the install completed, find the affected tarball URLs, and check the dependency layer before compiling the application. The repair changes the public-package URL prefix and adds build checks. Package versions, integrity values, application code, and Vite configuration stay the same.

Table of Contents

  • Before You Begin

  • How the Build Reached the Failure

  • Step 1: Check Whethernpm ciInstalled Anything

  • Step 2: Find Where the Lockfile Would Download Packages

  • Step 3: Rewrite Only the Known Public-package URL Prefix

  • Step 4: Apply the Guard at Every Independent Install

  • Step 5: Verify the Dependency Tree and the Trust Boundary

  • References

Before You Begin

You need a Node.js project with 

package.json
, a version 2 or 3 
package-lock.json
, its container build log, and Docker. The example uses a supported Node 24 image and a Vite project that writes its build output to 
dist
. Check your own dependency compatibility and output directory.

Check whether the affected packages come from a public or private registry before changing any URLs. The 

.invalid
hostname below stands in for the original internal host. Adapt that prefix only after reviewing the packages it serves.

How the Build Reached the Failure

The application came from a browser-hosted development environment and later moved into an Azure Container Registry build. The development platform acted as a proxy for public npm packages. When it regenerated 

package-lock.json
, it stored its own internal tarball URLs in the 
resolved
fields.

The failure crossed two environments:

  • Inside the development environment, npm could reach the package proxy. The lockfile kept those proxy URLs.

  • The Azure Container Registry image builder received the same lockfile, but it couldn't resolve the proxy hostname.

  • The dependency install printed 

    Exit handler never called!
    and left 
    node_modules
    empty. Its failure status didn't stop the next Docker layer in this incident.

  • The next layer ran 

    npm run build
    , which called Vite. With no installed Vite executable, the build reported 
    vite: not found
    .

The checks below follow that chain backward from the missing executable to the package locations, then repair the URLs and guard each independent install.

Figure 1. The container build reported the last failure in the chain.

Step 1: Check Whether 
npm ci
Installed Anything

The project used 

npm ci
, which was the correct command for a repeatable container build. npm's documentation says that the command removes an existing 
node_modules
directory before it starts the install. It also treats the lockfile as frozen instead of updating it.

Those properties made this failure unusually clear. The build couldn't fall back to packages from an earlier local install. Once the tarball downloads failed, the dependency directory contained nothing useful.

The Dockerfile separated dependency installation from source compilation. Step 3 compares that original sequence with the revised build.

The later 

vite: not found
message didn't show whether npm had installed the package. Start with the dependency directory in the same environment that failed:
test -d node_modules && find node_modules -mindepth 1 -maxdepth 1 | head
test -x node_modules/.bin/vite

In this build, the first check found no installed packages. The second confirmed that the Vite executable was missing. A missing binary can also result from omitting development dependencies, so inspect the directory before changing 

NODE_ENV
or the package manifest.

After a successful install, the directory listing should show package names. The 

test -x
command prints nothing. Immediately after it, inspect its exit status:
echo $?

For a missing Vite executable, the expected result is:

1

A result of 

0
means the executable exists and is executable.

Checkpoint: An empty dependency directory points to the install step. If other packages exist but Vite is missing, also check whether the install omitted development dependencies. These commands inspect the dependency directory without changing it.

Step 2: Find Where the Lockfile Would Download Packages

A generalized entry looked like this:

{
  "node_modules/example-package": {
    "version": "1.2.3",
    "resolved": "http://packages.internal.invalid/npm/example-package/-/example-package-1.2.3.tgz",
    "integrity": "sha512-"
  }
}

The 

.invalid
hostname above replaces the real internal hostname. The structure matches the historical lockfile.

npm documents 

resolved
as the location from which it obtained a package. For a registry package, that value can be a tarball URL. The configured registry on the build runner therefore didn't solve this incident. The lockfile already told npm where to fetch each tarball.

I counted the affected entries in the historical file. Of 1,038 dependency entries, 528 carried the internal hostname. Each pointed at a host that didn't resolve in the external build environment.

The npm debug output pointed to an earlier failure. The hostname failures appeared before 

Exit handler never called!
. That order mattered. The exit-handler message described how npm ended, while the failed downloads explained why the dependency tree was empty.

I inspected the lockfile as data instead of searching for one package name. This small script groups every HTTP 

resolved
value by hostname:
const fs = require('node:fs')
const lock = JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync('package-lock.json', 'utf8'))
const hosts = {}

for (const entry of Object.values(lock.packages ?? {})) {
  if (!entry.resolved?.startsWith('http')) continue
  const host = new URL(entry.resolved).host
  hosts[host] = (hosts[host] ?? 0) + 1
}

console.table(hosts)

That inventory showed that the problem affected 528 entries rather than one broken tarball. It also made the repair boundary clear. The package locations recorded in 

resolved
needed to change, while versions and integrity values stayed the same. If the host list includes a private registry, stop here and identify which packages it serves before rewriting anything.

The historical inventory contained this row. The table uses the replacement hostname from the example:

HostResolved URLs
packages.internal.invalid
 528

Your hostnames and counts will depend on your lockfile. This inventory counts HTTP tarball locations, so its total can differ from the number of dependency entries.

Checkpoint: Identify the unreachable host and confirm which of its packages come from the public npm registry. Record the affected count before choosing a replacement prefix. A hostname count alone doesn't establish that rewriting those URLs is safe.

Step 3: Rewrite Only the Known Public-package URL Prefix

Regenerating the lockfile can mix a registry repair with dependency updates. Keeping the package versions and integrity values unchanged makes the repair easier to review.

The affected packages in this application came from the public npm registry. The development platform proxied them and preserved their integrity values. The historical repair replaced its URL prefix before the container install.

For this walkthrough, save the following as 

rewrite-lockfile.cjs
. It changes only 
resolved
fields with the approved prefix. It checks for missing integrity values and unexpected paths on the old host before writing the file.
const fs = require('node:fs')

const oldPrefix = 'http://packages.internal.invalid/npm/'
const newPrefix = 'https://registry.npmjs.org/'
const oldHostname = new URL(oldPrefix).hostname
const filename = 'package-lock.json'
const lock = JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync(filename, 'utf8'))

if (!lock.packages || typeof lock.packages !== 'object') {
  throw new Error('Expected a lockfile with a packages object (version 2 or 3)')
}

let rewritten = 0
for (const entry of Object.values(lock.packages)) {
  if (typeof entry.resolved !== 'string') continue
  if (!entry.resolved.startsWith(oldPrefix)) continue
  if (!entry.integrity) throw new Error('An affected package has no integrity value')
  entry.resolved = newPrefix + entry.resolved.slice(oldPrefix.length)
  rewritten += 1
}

for (const entry of Object.values(lock.packages)) {
  if (typeof entry.resolved !== 'string') continue
  if (!entry.resolved.startsWith('http')) continue
  if (new URL(entry.resolved).hostname === oldHostname) {
    throw new Error('The old hostname remains under an unexpected URL prefix')
  }
}

fs.writeFileSync(filename, JSON.stringify(lock, null, 2) + '\n')
console.log(`Rewrote ${rewritten} resolved URLs`)

When the dependency stage runs the script, its message should match the number of URLs that use the approved prefix. The small test project used to check this tutorial produced:

Rewrote 40 resolved URLs

That test project is separate from the historical application, which had 528 affected entries. Use the inventory for your own file as the expected count. A zero count on an already-repaired file is expected. If an unrepaired file produces zero, check the prefix.

The script doesn't establish that a package is public. Confirm that separately. npm's integrity check then verifies that the downloaded bytes match the lockfile.

Keep local dependencies and configuration files out of the build context with a 

.dockerignore
:
node_modules
dist
.git
.env*
.npmrc

This example installs public packages. A private registry needs its own reachable endpoint and secure build-time authentication.

The first block below shows the affected instructions from the original Dockerfile. The second is the complete tutorial build. It uses Node 24 and the guarded install, so check compatibility with your own application.

Before: Original Install and Build Sequence

COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci

COPY . .
RUN npm run build

After: URL Rewrite and Dependency Checks

Use two build stages so source changes don't invalidate the dependency-install stage:

FROM node:24-slim AS dependencies
WORKDIR /app

COPY package.json package-lock.json rewrite-lockfile.cjs ./
RUN node rewrite-lockfile.cjs \
 && npm ci --include=dev \
 && test -x node_modules/.bin/vite

FROM node:24-slim AS build
WORKDIR /app

COPY . .
COPY --from=dependencies /app/node_modules ./node_modules
COPY --from=dependencies /app/package-lock.json ./package-lock.json
RUN npm run build

The revised Dockerfile makes each part of the install explicit:

  • The URL rewrite replaces the approved public-package prefix before 

    npm ci
    downloads packages. 

  • --include=dev
    makes the choice to install development dependencies explicit.

  • The Vite executable check stops the dependency stage if the install leaves Vite missing.

  • The separate dependency stage installs packages before the application build stage copies them and compiles the source.

The second stage copies the repaired lockfile after the application source. Otherwise, 

COPY . .
would put the original lockfile back into the build image. The 
.dockerignore
also prevents local 
node_modules
from overwriting the dependencies from the first stage.

--include=dev
includes Vite when it's a development dependency, even if the build environment sets 
NODE_ENV=production
. This image is a build environment, so it needs the compiler and build tools. Choose a supported Node version compatible with your project.

The historical lockfile comparison found 528 changed fields, all named 

resolved
. It found zero changed 
version
or 
integrity
fields and no remaining internal hostname. The example script above also leaves unrelated fields unchanged, although JSON formatting can change.

Figure 2. The portability repair changes package locations while preserving dependency identity.

The executable check makes the dependency stage fail if Vite is still missing. Docker stops at that stage instead of reaching the application build.

Checkpoint: Check the rewrite count against your inventory, confirm that the approved old hostname is gone, and compare versions and integrity values before and after the repair. The dependency stage must complete both 

npm ci --include=dev
and the Vite executable check. Step 5 builds the image and verifies the application output.

Step 4: Apply the Guard at Every Independent Install

The continuous integration job and the container image builder ran separate installs. Fixing the workflow runner didn't change the 

npm ci
inside the Dockerfile. The image build received the original repository files and created its own dependency layer in another environment.

The rewrite belongs immediately after the dependency files enter the install environment. Docker's cache guidance recommends installing dependencies before copying frequently changing source files. In the example, the dependency stage has that boundary. A source-only change rebuilds the application stage.

Apply the same guard before each independent install:

  • the continuous integration type-check install

  • the container build install

  • any runtime-stage install in a multi-stage Dockerfile

Figure 3. A workflow repair doesn't automatically repair the install inside a container build.

This placement also prevented a misleading partial fix. A type check could otherwise pass while the image build failed because the two jobs used the same lockfile in separate installs.

Step 5: Verify the Dependency Tree and the Trust Boundary

This repair was safe because the affected entries represented public npm packages behind a transparent development-platform proxy. The integrity strings remained present, and the rewrite didn't change any package version.

The same substitution would be unsafe for private packages, patched packages, or a registry that serves different bytes under the same package version. A portable build should keep those packages on a reachable private registry and configure authentication for that registry.

Before applying this pattern elsewhere, I would inventory every 

resolved
hostname and separate public packages from private ones. I would then compare package versions and integrity values before and after the change. The build should fail if an unapproved hostname remains.

An npm CLI issue records the same 

Exit handler never called!
message after package downloads from an internal registry timed out. That message doesn't identify the package location by itself. In this incident, the tarball URLs and failed hostname established the cause.

Build the image and verify the output:

docker build --progress=plain -t vite-install-check .
docker run --rm vite-install-check sh -c \
  'test -x node_modules/.bin/vite && test -s dist/index.html'

The build must pass 

npm ci
, the Vite executable check, and 
npm run build
. The final command checks the expected Vite output in the resulting image. Adapt the output check if your project uses a different directory. The image in this example compiles the application. Choose a separate serving stage if you need a production web server.

A successful minimal example doesn't validate every dependency in an existing application. Run the same build against the project you intend to ship. When a tool is missing, check the install result and its earlier errors before changing the build tool.

entries.title: Build a Hybrid Search Engine in PostgreSQL: BM25 + Vector Retrieval
entries.summary: Most application search setups force a trade-off: settle for simple text filters, or manage a separate search cluster like Elasticsearch with complex synchronization pipelines. In a new video course o
entries.content:
Most application search setups force a trade-off: settle for simple text filters, or manage a separate search cluster like Elasticsearch with complex synchronization pipelines.

In a new video course on the freeCodeCamp.org YouTube channel, I demonstrate how to run an entire production-grade search pipeline inside PostgreSQL. By pairing lexical keyword matching with dense vector embeddings in a single database, you eliminate external dependencies while preserving ACID guarantees for your search index.

Search queries usually demand two different retrieval behaviors. Exact queries like 

"Apollo 13"
require precise keyword matching, which keyword engines handle best. Conceptual queries like 
"animals that make their own light"
describe an idea without naming bioluminescence, which is where semantic vector search excels. Hybrid search executes both strategies simultaneously and uses Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) in SQL to merge the results into one ranked list.

In this course I build a complete full-stack search application over 240,000 Simple English Wikipedia articles. The tutorial covers setting up the 

pg_textsearch
extension for corpus-aware BM25 ranking, storing 384-dimensional sentence embeddings with 
pgvector
and 
pgvectorscale
, and profiling query plans with 
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
. The backend ties everything together using Python, FastAPI, and Psycopg, featuring match highlighting and single-transaction document writes.

Watch the PostgreSQL Hybrid Search Course on freeCodeCamp.org (1-hour watch).

entries.title: How Neural Networks Work: Why Straight Lines Aren't Enough
entries.summary: A straight line equation is a good place to start understanding how a neural network works. It's what we explored in my previous article, How Neural Networks Work – Explained Using the Straight Line E
entries.content:
A straight line equation is a good place to start understanding how a neural network works. It's what we explored in my previous article, How Neural Networks Work – Explained Using the Straight Line Equation (y=ax+b).

But, what if the relationship between the input and the output isn't linear?

We all know that in the real world, the data doesn't always follow a straight line pattern. This is where things start getting interesting: sometimes a single rule isn't enough to describe the relationship between the variables.

That’s where non-linearity comes in. It allows neural networks to capture changing behaviour in data.

In this article, we'll explore the concept of non-linearity that can capture complex relationships in data. Using a simple example, we'll try to understand piecewise linear curves, ReLU functions, S-shaped curves, and sigmoid functions in relation to how they help neural networks learn patterns that a straight line can't describe.

Table of Contents

  • Prerequisites

  • When a Straight Line Is Enough

  • When a Straight Line Isn't Enough

  • Modelling a Deep Neural Network

  • Final Thoughts

Prerequisites

  • Basic understanding of linear functions

  • Familiarity with the concept of deep neural networks

When a Straight Line Is Enough

A straight line equation means that the same rule applies throughout the relationship.

y = ax + b

y => Output variable
x => Input variable
a => Amount by which y changes when x changes (slope)
b => Value of y when x is 0 (y intercept)

We can look at an example to understand it better.

Ms. Poly is a math teacher who wants to come up with a study plan for her students to help them ace the final exam. She creates a rule of thumb using one factor: the number of hours studied per week. This means that the mark scored by a student is directly proportionate to the hours they spend studying.

Based on her assumption, she comes up with an equation in the form y=ax+b.

y => Marks scored
x => Number of hours studied
a => Increase in marks for every hour studied
b => Minimum marks every student is capable of scoring without studying.

So, after a quarterly exam, she interviews her students and collects information on how many hours they studied math per week. She creates a table with two columns: number of hours studied (x) per week and marks scored (y) and plots them.

Number of Hours StudiedMarks Scored
040
140
241
340
448
558
669
780
880

But when she tries to apply her simple formula, it doesn't seem to align with the data she collected, proving that real-life data is rarely that straightforward.

When a Straight Line Isn't Enough

Ms. Poly observes the graph closely and identifies a few patterns. Students who study for only a few hours may not see much improvement. Once they cross a certain point, their marks begin to increase with additional study. And again after a certain point, the marks remain fairly constant.

Thus, Ms Poly’s simple straight line equation isn’t enough to describe the relation between number of hours studied (x) per week and marks scored (y).

Instead, it can be divided into three parts,

Less than t₁ hours: Marks remain constant
t₁ to t₂ hours: Marks increase with study time
More than t₂ hours: Marks remain constant

So, she can have separate equations for each range and write them like this:

y = 1st equation, x=t₂

This example gives us our first glimpse of non-linearity. There are changes in the relationship at specific points, so a single straight line equation is insufficient as the behaviour needs to change at different points.

A simple way to handle this is using a piecewise linear function.

Piecewise Linear Curve

To begin with, for simplicity, Ms. Poly decides to consider only two regions.

Region1: Hours of study < t₁
Region2: Hours of study >= t₁

The values in the first region hover around a particular value. Even though they don’t lie perfectly in a line, she can make an approximation and represent that region as a line with slope=0. This indicates that the marks remain roughly the same.

In the second region, there seems to be a positive slope. So she decides on another straight line equation for that steep upward sloping line.

Ms. Poly ends up having two equations for the above graph because one equation can't define it. The rule changes for different ranges as the pattern changes.

So, she can write it like this:

y = 1st equation, x=t₁

Individually, these may seem like straight line equations. But when put together, the overall relationship is no longer a straight line. When x crosses a certain value, the equation changes. This is called piecewise linear function. It's a function that's made up of different rules for different ranges of input.

This idea appears in one of the most widely used activation functions in neural networks: ReLU.

What is a ReLU Function?

ReLU stands for Rectified Linear Unit. Mathematically, it's this:

y = ReLU(x) = max(0,x)

It keeps positive inputs unchanged and turns negative inputs to zero.

Here too, the individual piece is linear but the overall function is non-linear. So, ReLU is a piecewise linear function that introduces non-linearity.

The graph below shows the ReLU function:

This simple change in behaviour allows a neuron to respond differently to different ranges of input, giving neural networks a way to move beyond a single straight-line relationship.

S-Shaped Curve

Now, a piecewise linear curve does the job but Ms. Poly sees that there's quite a sharp transition from one region to the other. She had also only considered two regions for simplicity, even though the distribution can be divided into three regions.

So, she draws a smooth curve roughly passing through all the points as shown below:

This shape shows that the marks remain almost the same when a student studies for up to t₁ number of hours. Then, an increase in hours of study from t₁ to t₂, increases the marks scored, so there's a slope. In the end at t₂, it flattens out again. This transition is gradual and continuous unlike the piecewise linear curve which changes directions using simple straight lines.

The curve that Ms Poly drew isn't some random pattern. It can be represented mathematically, too. One of the functions that produces this kind of shape is the sigmoid function.

What is a Sigmoid Function?

A sigmoid function is a mathematical formula that takes any real-valued input and maps it to values between 0 and 1. It slowly increases from values close to 0, rises quickly in the middle and gradually levels off at values close to 1.

y = σ(x) = 1 / (1 + exp(-x))

The graph below shows the sigmoid function:

The sigmoid function is significant in neural networks because it introduces non-linearity while also restricting the output between 0 and 1. This makes it useful when the output needs to represent a probability such as the likelihood of a student passing an exam. A higher sigmoid output indicates a higher probability of the student passing, and vice versa.

Modeling a Deep Neural Network

Ms Poly should now combine the concepts of linear and non-linear equations to model a deep neural network. She has to take two separate approaches to ,

  • Predict the marks scored in the exam

  • Predict Pass/Fail in the exam

She uses two very simple untrained neural networks with manually chosen weights and biases for each. She is just trying it out to illustrate how calculations work. In reality she wouldn't choose the parameters herself. She would set up the network with weights and biases being learnt during training by repeatedly comparing the predicted values with the actual values and adjusting the parameters to minimise the error.

Predicting Marks Using ReLU

Step #1: Set up the network

Ms Poly has the set up the deep neural network with simple equations in the following way:

  • Input Layer: The number of hours studied (x) is received here.

  • Hidden Layer: Linear transformation and ReLU is applied to the input.

    z = w₁x + b₁, = x - 3      (w₁=1, b₁=-3)
h = ReLU(z) = max(0, z)

  • Output Layer: The marks scored is predicted after applying a linear transformation to the hidden layer's output(h).

    ŷ = w₂h + b₂ = 10h + 40      (w₂=10, b₂=40)

Step #2: Calculate the Predicted Marks

Suppose she wants to calculate the marks scored by a student who studies for 5 hours. This is how she does it:

z = w₁x + b₁, = x - 3 = 5 - 3 = 2
h = ReLU(z) = max(0, z) = max(0, 2) = 2

Finally calculate the predicted marks:

ŷ = w₂h + b₂ = 10h + 40 = 10(2) + 40 = 60

The neural network predicts 60 marks whereas the actual marks in the dataset is 58.

Step #3: Compare Predictions with Actual Marks

After Ms Poly gets all the marks predicted by the neural network, she compares them with the actual data in the table below:

Number of Hours StudiedMarks ScoredPredicted Marks
04040
14040
24140
34040
44850
55860
66970
78080
88090

The actual and predicted marks don't match exactly, but they're close. The marks keep increasing and don't flatten out in the end because the value keeps increasing after the ReLU threshold.

Through this example Ms Poly has demonstrated how ReLU helps in modeling non-linear relationships in the data.

Predicting Pass/Fail Using ReLU and Sigmoid

Here Ms Poly will use a neural network to predict whether a student passes or fails in the final exam. She assumes a student needs to score a minimum of 50 marks to pass. This network will be used to predict the probability of passing the exam.

Step #1: Set Up the Network

Ms Poly has the set up the deep neural network with simple equations in the following way:

  • Input Layer: The number of hours studied (x) is received here.

  • Hidden Layer: Linear transformation and ReLU is applied to the input.

    z₁ = w₁x + b₁, = x - 4      (w₁=1, b₁=-4)
h = ReLU(z₁) = max(0, z₁)

  • Output Layer: The pass/fail is predicted after applying sigmoid activation to the linear transformation of the hidden layer's output(h).

    z₂ = w₂h + b₂ = 2h - 1      (w₂=2, b₂=-1)
p = σ(z₂) = 1 / (1 + exp(-z₂))
ŷ = Pass, if p >= 0.5
ŷ = Fail, if p < 0.5

Step #2: Calculate the Pass/Fail Prediction

Suppose she wants to predict the result for a student who studies for 3 hours. This is how she does it:

z₁ = w₁x + b₁, = x - 4 = 3 - 4 = -1
h = ReLU(z₁) = max(0, z₁) = max(0, -1) = 0

Predicting if the student passes/fails:

z₂ = w₂h + b₂ = 2h - 1 = 2(0) - 1 = -1
p = σ(z₂) = 1 / (1 + exp(-z₂)) = 1 / (1 + exp(-(-1))) ≈ 0.269

Since 0.269<0.5, the student's result is Fail.

Now for the result of a student who studies for 5 hours:

z₁ = w₁x + b₁, = x - 4 = 5 - 4 = 1
h = ReLU(z₁) = max(0, z₁) = max(0, 1) = 1

Predicting if the student passes/fails:

z₂ = w₂h + b₂ = 2h - 1 = 2(1) - 1 = 1
p = σ(z₂) = 1 / (1 + exp(-z₂)) = 1 / (1 + exp(-1)) ≈ 0.731

Since 0.731>0.5, the student's result is Pass.

Step #3: Compare Predictions with Actual Results

Number of Hours StudiedMarks ScoredActual ResultPredicted ScorePredicted Result
040Fail0.269Fail
140Fail0.269Fail
241Fail0.269Fail
340Fail0.269Fail
448Fail0.269Fail
558Pass0.731Pass
669Pass0.953Pass
780Pass0.993Pass
880Pass0.999Pass

The network correctly classifies the result of all the students in this example. As the study hours increase beyond 4, the predicted score increases, making pass prediction more likely.

Through this example Ms Poly has demonstrated how ReLU and sigmoid work together. ReLU transforms the input in the hidden layer and sigmoid helps in converting the output to a score that can be used to make Pass/Fail prediction.

Final Thoughts

The simple examples shown above help us understand an important rule about neural networks: the relationship between the outputs and the inputs can behave differently across different parts of the input. They need to be captured in order to produce meaningful results from real-world data.

A straight line equation is enough when the relationship in data is simple and consistent. But real-life data isn't always that straightforward. By introducing non-linearity, neural networks can move beyond straight-line relationships and learn complex relationships hidden in data.

entries.content:
Your smart ring or watch has many useful jobs, including learning your usual physiological patterns and showing you when they change.

Resting heart rate, heart rate variability (HRV), temperature, and breathing rate can all contribute to that picture, although each device interprets these measurements differently.

That works well until pregnancy changes what usual looks like for several of those metrics.

The first app I open every morning is Oura, so I know how much one score can shape my day. A low Readiness Score can make me feel like I've done something wrong, even when I haven't. Now imagine seeing that for weeks while your body is going through expected physiological changes.

That's what I want to look at here, and I've pulled in the research so you don't have to take my word for it.

Table of Contents

  • Why Your Baseline Stops Making Sense

  • What Actually Changes?

  • How Major Wearables Handle Pregnancy

  • What Pregnancy-Aware Wearables Still Need

  • Wrapping Up

Why Your Baseline Stops Making Sense

Most wearables use a combination of personal trends and device-specific reference ranges to interpret your measurements. The problem is that pregnancy changes several physiological metrics, and a baseline established before pregnancy may not reflect what's expected at a particular stage of pregnancy.

Oura, for example, gives people who join while already pregnant a calibration window of 7 to 15 days so the app can establish a personal baseline. Its current support guidance describes a period of 7 to 14 days of consistent ring wear before Pregnancy Trends become available.

The distinction matters because a baseline established during pregnancy may represent that stage of pregnancy, rather than your pre-pregnancy physiology.

Pregnancy can change cardiovascular measurements quite early. Cardiac output, the amount of blood the heart pumps per minute, increases during pregnancy, as does heart rate. The magnitude and timing vary between individuals, so these changes shouldn't be treated as a fixed curve that everyone follows.

A 2023 study published in Sensors also discusses research showing that resting heart rate can rise by 10 to 20 beats per minute, with changes beginning as early as weeks 5 to 7. But that increase isn't universal, and the trajectory varies across studies.

A system that relies too heavily on pre-pregnancy measurements may interpret expected changes as unusual. But pregnancy doesn't make every abnormal reading harmless, either. The challenge is helping users understand what their data might mean without treating a consumer wellness score as a medical assessment.

What Actually Changes?

Let's get into it. Much of this research involves small samples and different devices, so treat the numbers as observations from specific studies, not predictions of what will happen to everyone.

Heart Rate and HRV

A study conducted at University Hospital Zurich followed 23 healthy pregnant women who wore a bracelet at night. Average resting heart rate rose from about 61 beats per minute at week 8 to about 67 by week 35. It sat around 66 between weeks 24 and 32 and dropped slightly near the end.

HRV, which measures variations in the time between consecutive heartbeats, declined across roughly the first two-thirds of pregnancy in this sample, then climbed back toward where it started. HRV is often used as one indicator of physiological recovery or stress, but it isn't a direct measure of either. Its interpretation depends on personal history, measurement methods, and other factors.

A WHOOP study involving active women, including research associated with West Virginia University, reported a similar pattern of declining HRV and rising resting heart rate. Activity levels affected how much these measurements changed. Regular exercise, therefore, doesn't necessarily prevent pregnancy-related changes in either metric.

WHOOP also shares a rower's account in which her average HRV went from 64 before pregnancy to 50 during the first six months. That's an individual example, not a typical trajectory for every pregnant person. Still, it raises an important question: what happens when a recovery score interprets a change from someone's usual HRV as a negative signal without enough pregnancy context?

A 2025 scoping review of six wearable HRV studies found a similar overall pattern: HRV tended to decline during pregnancy and move back toward pre-pregnancy levels postpartum. But the studies differed in their methods, and the findings don't establish one expected HRV curve for everyone.

Temperature

This one is trickier because the results depend on what you measure, where you measure it, and when.

A 2024 study published in npj Digital Medicine analyzed Oura Ring data from 120 people, including 97 full-term pregnancies. After conception, nightly peak skin-temperature measurements rose above pre-pregnancy levels before gradually declining. Nightly lowest measurements followed a different pattern, dipping early in pregnancy and then rising towards delivery.

These were skin-temperature measurements recorded by a wearable, not direct measurements of core body temperature.

The Zurich bracelet study measured wrist skin temperature during sleep and found relatively little change across pregnancy. The authors discuss how skin blood flow and the conditions under which measurements are taken may help explain this result.

The two studies used different devices, measurement sites, and methods, so their results aren't directly interchangeable.

This is why "your temperature is up" doesn't mean the same thing in week 6 as it does in week 36. A useful wearable needs to account for the measurement method and the stage of pregnancy before interpreting a temperature trend. A change in skin temperature alone also can't establish whether someone has an infection or another medical condition.

Breathing and Sleep

In the Zurich study, breathing rate rose from about 12 breaths per minute around weeks 9 and 10 to about 16 around week 17, then eased down later. This was the pattern observed in that small sample, rather than a universal trajectory for pregnancy.

Sleep changes too. A 2026 study in Frontiers in Global Women's Health tracked 14 women with an Oura ring over 981 observation days. As pregnancy progressed, deep sleep began later and occurred less frequently, while time spent awake increased.

More deep sleep was associated with lower heart rate and higher HRV, while REM sleep showed the opposite associations. These are associations, not proof that one sleep stage causes a particular cardiovascular response. The sample was also small, so the findings need further study.

Still, the results raise a practical question. An app that treats reduced deep sleep as an isolated negative signal may fail to communicate how sleep patterns can change during pregnancy. A sleep score should help users understand their trends, not imply that every change represents poor recovery.

How Major Wearables Handle Pregnancy

Several major wearable companies now offer pregnancy-related features, although their approaches differ.

Oura launched Pregnancy Insights in August 2025. It tracks temperature trends, resting heart rate, HRV and respiratory rate across pregnancy, with pregnancy-specific context to help users interpret these measurements. Users can also record symptoms and experiences, including nausea and Braxton Hicks contractions.

Oura's Pregnancy Insights documentation describes the feature's introduction, while its support guidance explains how pregnancy trends and Readiness contributors are presented.

WHOOP has its own Pregnancy Insights. Users enter their due date to receive weekly guidance, and the feature provides pregnancy-related recovery context for up to 12 weeks postpartum. WHOOP also makes clear that its wearable can't detect or diagnose pregnancy. Its pregnancy coaching guide explains the feature and its intended use.

Apple added pregnancy-related tracking support with watchOS 11 and iOS 18. After a user logs a pregnancy in the Health app, Cycle Tracking can display gestational age on Apple Watch. Apple also prompts users to review high-heart-rate notification settings if the threshold is set below 120 bpm. Its guidance recommends turning off Cardio Fitness notifications during pregnancy and until 12 weeks after pregnancy ends.

I read that last recommendation as a reminder that standard health metrics and notifications may need different handling during pregnancy. But Apple's pregnancy logging and notification adjustments aren't the same as the pregnancy-specific trend analysis offered by Oura or the coaching offered by WHOOP.

These are useful steps, but the features shouldn't be treated as equivalent. Each company uses different measurements, algorithms, and forms of guidance, and none of these features replace clinical assessment.

What Pregnancy-Aware Wearables Still Need

This part is my wish list, based on the research and the gaps I see in how consumer wearables communicate health data.

Exercise Intensity

ACOG's guidance says perceived exertion may be more useful than heart-rate targets for monitoring exercise intensity during pregnancy, since heart-rate responses to exercise can be regular or blunted. Its exercise guidance discusses the use of perceived exertion and the talk test.

Most strain and training scores rely heavily on heart rate. I'd like a pregnancy mode that offers a talk-test prompt or a quick effort rating alongside heart-rate data, rather than relying on heart-rate zones alone.

The aim shouldn't be to discard heart-rate measurements. It should be to give them the right context and help users interpret exercise intensity using more than one signal.

Curves, Not a Straight Line

The research shows that HRV may fall and then rise, breathing rate can change at different stages, and temperature patterns vary depending on what the device measures. A system that relies only on recent trends could misinterpret a late-pregnancy rise in HRV as improved recovery unless it accounts for gestational age and the wider pattern.

Oura already places pregnancy trends alongside reference patterns observed during pregnancy, which is a useful step. I'd like every brand to build on this approach by comparing measurements with both the user's own history and appropriate reference ranges for the relevant stage of pregnancy.

That would require more than assigning every pregnant user the same expected curve. Companies would need validated reference data, consistent measurement methods and testing across different populations. They would also need to account for missing data and explain when the available measurements aren't enough to draw a clear conclusion.

Different Devices, Different Curves

Not every sensor measures the same thing in the same way. Oura measures skin temperature at the finger, while the Zurich bracelet study measured wrist skin temperature. The studies produced different temperature patterns, but differences in sensor location, measurement methods, and study design make a direct comparison difficult.

This is worth remembering when comparing your numbers with charts you find online from another device. A difference between two readings doesn't automatically mean that one device is wrong. The measurements may reflect different signals.

I'd like companies to explain what their sensors measure, how they process the data, and which comparisons are appropriate. That information would make it easier for users to understand what a trend can and cannot tell them.

Symptoms Need a Seat at the Table

Nausea, food aversions, Braxton Hicks contractions and plain exhaustion are exactly the kind of context that can help explain an unusual morning score. The Zurich study also linked self-reported feelings such as stress and tiredness with changes in HRV and breathing rate.

Oura already offers a way to record this context through its Pregnancy Insights symptom tags. In the app's Keeping Track section, users can log symptoms, activities, emotions and other factors that may affect how they feel during pregnancy. Examples include nausea, heartburn, vomiting, and Braxton Hicks contractions. These tags can be viewed alongside biometric trends, helping users identify patterns over time. They don't directly change daily scores or prove that a particular symptom caused a change in HRV, heart rate or sleep.

I'd like to see this feature go one step further with a one-tap check-in when a score changes noticeably, making it easier to record relevant symptoms at the time. That context could help users interpret their trends more clearly, without treating symptoms as a reason to dismiss unusual readings or replacing medical advice.

That doesn't mean symptoms should be used to dismiss unusual readings. Instead, they should help the app explain the data more clearly and identify when a trend needs attention rather than simply assigning a lower score.

Alerts That Need a Gentler Voice

Routine prenatal visits may be separated by several weeks, depending on gestational age and individual needs. Continuous wearable measurements could provide additional observations between appointments, but more data doesn't automatically lead to better clinical decisions.

Researchers have suggested that HRV could be worth studying as a potential signal associated with hypertensive disorders, while temperature measurements could contribute to research into infection detection.

But the evidence discussed here doesn't establish either metric as a validated standalone screening tool for these conditions. Larger studies and clinical validation are needed before such alerts can be relied on.

Getting an unexplained notification about a physiological change can cause a pregnant person unnecessary concern, particularly when an app can't establish whether that change is clinically significant. If pregnancy-related alerts are introduced, the wording needs care. The app should explain what changed, acknowledge uncertainty, and provide appropriate guidance on when to contact a healthcare professional.

Postpartum

Your baseline changes again after birth. WHOOP offers pregnancy-related guidance for up to 12 weeks postpartum, while Apple recommends turning off Cardio Fitness notifications during pregnancy and for 12 weeks afterward.

These product settings recognize that pregnancy-related changes can extend beyond delivery, but they shouldn't be interpreted as a universal physiological recovery timeline. The 2025 HRV review found that HRV tended to return toward pre-pregnancy levels postpartum, but individual recovery patterns vary.

A device shouldn't automatically treat your pre-pregnancy numbers as the only reference point on day one after birth. It should account for postpartum trends and allow time for measurements to change. And honestly, with a newborn at home, sleep data needs a fair amount of context too.

Wrapping Up

Baseline tracking only works if the baseline is allowed to change. Pregnancy affects several physiological measurements in patterns researchers are still working to understand, and Oura, WHOOP, and Apple have all introduced features to address parts of the problem.

My wish list is short: reference ranges by gestational week, exercise guidance that considers perceived effort, sleep scoring that accounts for changes in sleep patterns, careful alerts, and a gradual return to pre-pregnancy comparisons after birth.

The next step is to validate these approaches across larger and more varied groups of pregnant users. Wearables need to explain changes clearly, account for individual differences, and distinguish unusual measurements from clinically meaningful signals.

And if you're pregnant and wearing one of these devices, discuss health concerns with your care team regardless of what your wearable reports. These devices can provide useful context, but they don't replace prenatal care.

I'm curious which brand will take the next step in making pregnancy-related health data easier to interpret.

entries.title: How to Build an AI Agent Harness from Scratch in TypeScript
