How katalepsis Works Under the Hood

A few of the decisions came straight out of the problems in this article. Here's how they work in the code.

katalepsis is a TypeScript monorepo with five packages:

  • core
    (the result schema, the Playwright runner, and the report renderers) 

  • agent
    (the browser tools and evidence rules for 
    verify
    ) 

  • credentials
    (keys and preferences) 

  • mcp
    (the MCP server) 

  • cli

It uses Effect for the parts where errors, cancellation, and dependencies matter, such as running Playwright and probing the preview, and Effect Schema for the report format. The model loop in 

verify
uses the Vercel AI SDK, so the same code works with Anthropic, OpenAI, and OpenRouter.

The Report is a Schema, Not a Log

Every run, whether it came from Playwright or from a model, decodes into the same 

VerificationRun
structure before anything is written. A trimmed version of a single check looks like this:
export const CheckStatus = Schema.Literals(["passed", "failed", "blocked"]);

export const VerificationCheck = Schema.Struct({
  id: Schema.String,
  source: Schema.Literals(["playwright-test", "agent"]),
  title: Schema.String,
  status: CheckStatus,
  flaky: Schema.Boolean,
  failure: Schema.NullOr(Schema.Struct({ code: FailureCode, message: Schema.String })),
  attempts: Schema.Array(Attempt),
  evidence: Schema.Array(BundlePath),
});

Tests that never ran go into a separate 

notTested
list with a reason, which is how you end up with four outcomes: passed, failed, blocked, or not tested. Every evidence file is stored with its SHA-256 hash, and 
BundlePath
rejects absolute paths and 
..
, so a report can't point outside its own folder.

Blocked isn't Failed

If the preview is down, you get one blocked run, not three failed tests that send you hunting for bugs that don't exist. Before starting Playwright, katalepsis requests the preview URL once. This is the core of that probe:

const UNAVAILABLE_STATUSES = new Set([502, 503, 504]);

const response = await fetch(url, {
  redirect: "manual",
  signal: AbortSignal.any([signal, AbortSignal.timeout(30_000)]),
});
if (UNAVAILABLE_STATUSES.has(response.status)) {
  return { reachable: false, reason: `the preview answered with HTTP ${response.status}` };
}

A network error or a gateway status blocks every selected test, and Playwright never starts. Pointing the demo at a port with nothing on it gives you this:

$ katalepsis run --cwd apps/demo-form --url http://127.0.0.1:4999
katalepsis: BLOCKED
  0 passed, 0 failed, 3 blocked, 0 not tested
  preview-unavailable: http://127.0.0.1:4999/ did not respond (connect ECONNREFUSED 127.0.0.1:4999). Playwright was not run.

Playwright's Verdict is Final

run
starts the project's own Playwright with 
--reporter=json
and reads the result file, rather than reimplementing anything. Playwright already marks a test that passed on retry as 
flaky
, so katalepsis keeps that flag and lists every attempt.

What it does add is classification. A failure whose message names the preview's own origin as unreachable becomes blocked, but a dead third-party API stays failed, because that's a real problem with your app. A browser that couldn't launch is blocked too, which is exactly what I got the first time I ran the demo for this article on a machine with the wrong browser build installed.

The Model Doesn't Get to Call Something a Pass

The model in 

verify
can click and type and read the page, but it doesn't get to call something a pass. A check only passes if the model points to a browser assertion that katalepsis ran, that passed, and that shows something that wasn't on the page before the model acted. Otherwise it comes back blocked.

Here's how that works. The model only gets a small set of tools: 

navigate
, 
snapshot
, 
click
, 
fill
, 
press
, 
assert
, and 
finish
. 
assert
doesn't return the model's opinion. katalepsis runs the check in the browser itself, takes a screenshot, and records the result with an ID like 
a3
. When the model calls 
finish
, it has to cite those IDs:
finish: tool({
  description: "Report the verdict once, citing assertion IDs such as a1.",
  inputSchema: schema(
    Schema.Struct({
      verdict: Schema.Literals(["passed", "failed", "blocked"]),
      summary: Schema.String,
      assertionIds: Schema.Array(Schema.String),
    }),
  ),
  execute: (verdict) => {
    onFinish(verdict);
    return "Recorded.";
  },
}),

Then a plain function, 

decideOutcome
, compares the claim with the evidence. A trimmed version of the pass rule:
if (!cited.every((assertion) => assertion.passed)) {
  return "The agent reported a pass, but a cited assertion failed.";
}
const shown = cited.filter((assertion) => assertion.expectation === "visible");
if (shown.length === 0) {
  return "The agent reported a pass citing only hidden or URL assertions.";
}
if (!observeOnly && shown.every((assertion) => assertion.trueAtStart === true)) {
  return "The agent reported a pass, but everything it cited was already on the page before it acted.";
}

Any of those messages turns the check into blocked with the code 

no-evidence
. Citing an assertion ID that never ran is blocked too. The function also blocks a pass if an uncited assertion failed after the last cited one, because the latest evidence disagrees with the verdict.

That 

trueAtStart
condition exists because one of the models I tested tried to prove a form worked by citing the label of the email field, which had been there all along. T

o catch it, each check opens two copies of the start page in separate browser contexts. The model works in one, and the other stays untouched. When the model asserts that something is visible, katalepsis looks for the same element on the untouched copy, and if it's there too, the assertion gets 

trueAtStart: true
and can't carry a pass on its own.

One Action at a Time

The first live runs also caught parallel tool calls stepping on each other, and a name ending up typed into the email field. Models like to send several tool calls at once, and two 

fill
calls racing each other type into whichever field has focus. The fix is a promise queue that every browser action goes through:
private exclusive(action: () => Promise): Promise {
  const next = this.queue.then(action, action);
  this.queue = next.catch(() => undefined);
  return next;
}

Each action waits for the previous one to settle, whether it succeeded or failed, and a failure doesn't poison the queue for the next action.

Budgets and Boundaries

Each agent check runs in its own browser context with tracing on, so the report always has a trace to replay. Navigation is limited to the preview's origin plus anything you allow with 

--allow-origin
. The model has a step limit (
--max-steps
, 15 by default), a token limit (
--max-tokens
, 200,000), and a time limit (
--check-timeout
, 120 seconds), and running out of any of them is reported as blocked with the reason, not as a failure. Query strings are redacted from URLs in the report.

How it Was Built

Before writing code, I wrote a build plan split into milestones. M0 was a review of how two of my earlier projects handled credentials and providers, plus the first architecture decision record and the monorepo tooling. M1 was the Playwright runner and the report, M2 was agent checks with your own key, and M3 was the MCP server. Each milestone ended with a fresh agent with no history reviewing the work against the plan, the same independent-reviewer rule from earlier in this article.

Those reviews shaped the tool more than the plan did. The first one came back with 15 findings, including the rule that only an unreachable preview counts as blocked while other hosts stay failed. The M2 review found that a model could get a pass by citing an assertion that proved nothing, which is where the stricter pass rule and the untouched copy of the page came from. The M3 review found that a client quitting mid-run left Playwright and its browsers running, and that a crafted symlink could let the report tool read files outside the project. All of those are fixed and covered by tests now.

What Happened When I Used It

Before telling anyone about it, I ran it against two of my own projects. Conclave's suite came back with 95 passed. A larger app came back with 137 passed and one failure, an assertion on a zoom level that was slightly off.

That was a test I already had and hadn't noticed was failing, so katalepsis didn't find the bug so much as make it impossible to miss. Both projects also hardcoded their 

baseURL
, which meant their tests never touched the URL I passed in. katalepsis now warns about that, because a green run against the wrong server is worse than no run.

After I posted it on LinkedIn, someone in the comments pointed out that the commit you have checked out isn't necessarily the commit the preview was built from. They were right, so the report now records both and marks them confirmed, mismatched, or unknown, and a mismatch blocks a run that would otherwise pass, since a green run against a stale preview tells you nothing about your diff.

The preview reports its commit with an 

x-commit-sha
response header or a 
<meta
tag, which the same probe that checks availability reads. If your host can't do either, you can pass 
--preview-commit
yourself.

I'm dogfooding it in the same instructions this article describes. The browser-review skill now tells my agents to run katalepsis first, and to fall back to plain browser automation for what it can't check yet: field values, persistence, console and network, and layout across viewports.

The first Codex session to pick that up went looking for a "katalepsis skill" because of how I'd worded the line in 

AGENTS.md
, didn't find one, and fell back to its old browser review. Wrong for a silly reason, but the fallback did exactly what it was supposed to, and the fix was saying plainly that katalepsis is a CLI and browser-review is the skill.

A few days later I used it on a real work branch, a change that made GeoJSON the main download button and moved CSV and KML into a dropdown. The agent stopped before running anything, because 

verify
sends page content to the model provider and my rules say it needs my OK before doing that for an app. That's the behavior I want

With seeded synthetic data and an explicit OK, the check passed: one visible primary button, and the other formats showing up once the dropdown opened, with the screenshots and trace in the report. The skill still keeps pages with real data on the fallback path.

Where I Landed

Not every task needs any of this. I don't need Playwright to confirm a Markdown typo got fixed, and a backend refactor that can't change what renders doesn't need Chromium. I do want it for components, forms, navigation, dialogs, client state, maps, filtering, responsive layout, persistence, and any user-visible bug fix.

My rule of thumb is that if you're making a claim about how the UI behaves at runtime, the runtime UI should be part of the evidence.

None of this replaces good tests, code review, or me looking at changes that matter. It just adds the feedback loop that was missing. The agent already has the repository and the shell, and it knows what it changed. With a browser it can start answering whether the thing it built actually works, and with a report it can show me instead of telling me. If it can write the button, it can click it and show me what happened before it says it's done.

katalepsis is MIT licensed and on GitHub. If an agent check ever gives you a result you don't believe, I'd like to hear about it.

entries.title: How to Build and Publish a Native Android App in 2026: From Jetpack Compose to the Google Play Store
entries.summary: Most Android tutorials stop at "it runs on the emulator." But getting an app from a blank project to a listing that real people can install from Google Play involves a second half that's rarely discus
entries.content:
Most Android tutorials stop at "it runs on the emulator." But getting an app from a blank project to a listing that real people can install from Google Play involves a second half that's rarely discussed in one place: release builds, signing keys, app bundles, store listings, policy forms, and a mandatory testing period for new developer accounts.

Android development has also changed a lot in the last few years. Jetpack Compose is now the default UI toolkit, XML layouts are legacy, Kotlin is the only language the official templates use, and Google Play has tightened its requirements for new developers.

Older guides that start with 

findViewById
or end with uploading an APK no longer match how things work.

This handbook walks through the whole path. You'll build a small but complete notes app with Jetpack Compose, Room, ViewModel, and Navigation 3, write a couple of tests, produce a signed release bundle, and then take it through the Google Play Console all the way to a production release.

Table of Contents

  • Prerequisites

  • What You Will Build

  • How to Set Up Your Development Environment

  • How to Create a New Compose Project

  • How to Configure Dependencies with a Version Catalog

  • How Jetpack Compose Thinks About UI

  • How to Structure the App

  • How to Store Data Locally with Room

  • How to Expose Data with a Repository and Application Class

  • How to Manage UI State with a ViewModel

  • How to Build the Note List Screen

  • How to Build the Note Editor Screen

  • How to Add Navigation with Navigation 3

  • How to Handle Theming and Edge-to-Edge Display

  • How to Test Your Composables

  • How to Prepare the App for Release

  • How to Create an Upload Key and Sign Your App

  • How to Build an Android App Bundle

  • How to Create a Google Play Developer Account

  • How to Create Your App in the Play Console

  • How to Complete the App Content Declarations

  • How to Set Up Your Store Listing

  • How to Run Internal and Closed Testing

  • How to Publish to Production

  • How to Ship Updates After Launch

  • Summary

Prerequisites

You should be comfortable with basic programming concepts and have at least read some Kotlin before. You don't need prior Android experience. Every Android-specific concept is explained as it comes up.

For tools, you need:

  • A computer running macOS, Windows, or Linux with at least 16 GB of RAM (8 GB works, but the emulator will be slow)

  • The latest stable version of Android Studio

  • A physical Android phone (optional for development, but required later for Play Console account verification)

  • A Google account and 25 USD for the one-time Google Play developer registration fee

What You Will Build

The sample app is called Quick Notes. It shows a list of notes sorted by the last time they were edited, and it lets you create a new note with a floating action button, tap a note to edit it, and delete notes. Everything is stored locally on the device in a SQLite database, so the app works offline and needs no backend.

A notes app sounds simple, but it touches every piece a real app needs: a list screen and a detail screen, navigation between them with a working back button, persistent storage, state that survives configuration changes such as screen rotation, and user input. Once you understand how these pieces fit together, you can swap the notes for anything else.

Here's the high level architecture you'll end up with:

+-------------------------------------------------------------+
|                         UI Layer                            |
|  MainActivity -> NavDisplay -> NoteListScreen               |
|                             -> NoteEditorScreen             |
|                  observes StateFlow, sends events           |
+------------------------------+------------------------------+
                               |
                               v
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
|                      NotesViewModel                         |
|      holds UI state, survives rotation, launches coroutines |
+------------------------------+------------------------------+
                               |
                               v
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
|                       Data Layer                            |
|   NoteRepository -> NoteDao -> NotesDatabase (Room/SQLite)  |
+-------------------------------------------------------------+

The diagram shows three layers stacked vertically, with arrows pointing down to show the direction of dependencies.

The UI layer at the top contains the activity and the two screens. It only talks to the ViewModel, never directly to the database.

The ViewModel in the middle owns the state that the screens display and survives events like rotation that would otherwise destroy the screen.

The data layer at the bottom wraps Room, which is a typed layer on top of SQLite. Data flows back up the stack as a 

Flow
of notes, so when the database changes, the UI updates automatically.

This is the layered architecture that Google recommends in its official app architecture guide.

How to Set Up Your Development Environment

Download Android Studio from developer.android.com/studio and run the installer. On first launch, the setup wizard downloads the Android SDK, the platform tools (including 

adb
), and a system image for the emulator. Accept the defaults unless you have a reason not to. Android Studio bundles its own JDK, so you don't need to install Java separately.

Once setup finishes, open the SDK Manager from Tools > SDK Manager and confirm that the latest stable Android platform is installed. At the time of writing, that means at least Android 16 (API level 36).

Google Play requires new apps and app updates to target a recent API level, and the requirement moves forward every year, usually at the end of August. Check the target API level requirements page before you start so you know which number to aim for.

Next, create an emulator from Tools > Device Manager. Pick a recent Pixel phone profile and the newest system image with Google Play services.

If you would rather test on a physical phone, enable Developer Options on the device by tapping Build number seven times in Settings > About phone, then turn on USB debugging (or Wireless debugging) in the Developer Options menu.

How to Create a New Compose Project

In Android Studio, choose File > New > New Project and select the Empty Activity template. This template is Compose-based. The similarly named "Empty Views Activity" uses the older XML layout system, so make sure you pick the right one.

Fill in the project details. The Name is what users see (Quick Notes). The Package name is the permanent, globally unique identifier for your app on Google Play, written in reverse domain format such as 

com.yourname.quicknotes
. Choose it carefully, because you can't change it after you publish. Set Minimum SDK to API 24, which covers nearly every active Android device, and leave the build configuration language as Kotlin DSL.

Click Finish and wait for the first Gradle sync to complete. The project you get looks roughly like this:

QuickNotes/
├── app/
│   ├── build.gradle.kts
│   ├── proguard-rules.pro
│   └── src/
│       ├── main/
│       │   ├── AndroidManifest.xml
│       │   ├── java/com/yourname/quicknotes/
│       │   │   ├── MainActivity.kt
│       │   │   └── ui/theme/
│       │   └── res/
│       ├── test/
│       └── androidTest/
├── gradle/
│   └── libs.versions.toml
├── build.gradle.kts
└── settings.gradle.kts

The tree shows the important files in a fresh project.

The 

app
folder is the single module that becomes your installable app, and its 
build.gradle.kts
holds the Android configuration (SDK levels, version numbers, dependencies).

src/main
contains production code, the 
AndroidManifest.xml
that declares your app's components to the system, and the 
res
folder for resources such as icons and strings.

The 

test
folder is for unit tests that run on your computer, while 
androidTest
is for tests that run on a device or emulator.

At the root, 

gradle/libs.versions.toml
is the version catalog where all dependency versions live, and 
settings.gradle.kts
lists the modules in the project. Kotlin files sit under a folder named 
java
for historical reasons, which is normal.

Press the green Run button. After a short build, the emulator should show "Hello Android!" on screen. That confirms your toolchain works.

How to Configure Dependencies with a Version Catalog

Modern Android projects keep every library version in one file, 

gradle/libs.versions.toml
, and refer to those libraries by alias from the build scripts.

Open the catalog and replace its contents with the following:

[versions]
agp = "9.0.0"
kotlin = "2.3.0"
ksp = "2.3.4"
composeBom = "2026.01.00"
activityCompose = "1.12.2"
lifecycle = "2.10.0"
navigation3 = "1.0.0"
room = "2.8.4"
serialization = "1.9.0"
junit = "4.13.2"
androidxJunit = "1.3.0"

[libraries]
androidx-activity-compose = { group = "androidx.activity", name = "activity-compose", version.ref = "activityCompose" }
androidx-compose-bom = { group = "androidx.compose", name = "compose-bom", version.ref = "composeBom" }
androidx-compose-ui = { group = "androidx.compose.ui", name = "ui" }
androidx-compose-ui-tooling = { group = "androidx.compose.ui", name = "ui-tooling" }
androidx-compose-ui-tooling-preview = { group = "androidx.compose.ui", name = "ui-tooling-preview" }
androidx-compose-ui-test-junit4 = { group = "androidx.compose.ui", name = "ui-test-junit4" }
androidx-compose-ui-test-manifest = { group = "androidx.compose.ui", name = "ui-test-manifest" }
androidx-compose-material3 = { group = "androidx.compose.material3", name = "material3" }
androidx-compose-material-icons-core = { group = "androidx.compose.material", name = "material-icons-core" }
androidx-lifecycle-viewmodel-compose = { group = "androidx.lifecycle", name = "lifecycle-viewmodel-compose", version.ref = "lifecycle" }
androidx-lifecycle-runtime-compose = { group = "androidx.lifecycle", name = "lifecycle-runtime-compose", version.ref = "lifecycle" }
androidx-navigation3-runtime = { group = "androidx.navigation3", name = "navigation3-runtime", version.ref = "navigation3" }
androidx-navigation3-ui = { group = "androidx.navigation3", name = "navigation3-ui", version.ref = "navigation3" }
androidx-room-runtime = { group = "androidx.room", name = "room-runtime", version.ref = "room" }
androidx-room-ktx = { group = "androidx.room", name = "room-ktx", version.ref = "room" }
androidx-room-compiler = { group = "androidx.room", name = "room-compiler", version.ref = "room" }
kotlinx-serialization-core = { group = "org.jetbrains.kotlinx", name = "kotlinx-serialization-core", version.ref = "serialization" }
junit = { group = "junit", name = "junit", version.ref = "junit" }
androidx-junit = { group = "androidx.test.ext", name = "junit", version.ref = "androidxJunit" }

[plugins]
android-application = { id = "com.android.application", version.ref = "agp" }
kotlin-compose = { id = "org.jetbrains.kotlin.plugin.compose", version.ref = "kotlin" }
kotlin-serialization = { id = "org.jetbrains.kotlin.plugin.serialization", version.ref = "kotlin" }
ksp = { id = "com.google.devtools.ksp", version.ref = "ksp" }
room = { id = "androidx.room", version.ref = "room" }

The catalog has three sections: 

[versions]
names each version number once. 
[libraries]
maps a short alias to a Maven coordinate, and 
[plugins]
does the same for Gradle plugins.

Gradle turns the dashes in each alias into dots, so 

androidx-room-runtime
becomes 
libs.androidx.room.runtime
in your build scripts. The Compose libraries have no version of their own because they get it from the Compose BOM (bill of materials), which pins a set of Compose libraries that are tested together. The Kotlin Compose compiler plugin shares its version with Kotlin itself, which has been the case since Kotlin 2.0.

KSP is the annotation processor Room uses to generate database code. The version numbers here were current when this article was written. Android Studio highlights outdated entries in the catalog, and you should accept its suggestions to move to the latest stable versions.

Now update the root 

build.gradle.kts
so the plugins are available to the app module:
plugins {
    alias(libs.plugins.android.application) apply false
    alias(libs.plugins.kotlin.compose) apply false
    alias(libs.plugins.kotlin.serialization) apply false
    alias(libs.plugins.ksp) apply false
    alias(libs.plugins.room) apply false
}

This file declares each plugin with 

apply false
, which puts the plugin on the build classpath without applying it to the root project. Each module then opts into the plugins it actually needs.

You might notice there's no 

org.jetbrains.kotlin.android
plugin. Starting with Android Gradle Plugin 9, Kotlin support is built into the Android plugin, so a separate Kotlin Android plugin is no longer required. If you're working in an older project on AGP 8, you'll still see that plugin applied, and that's fine.

Then replace the contents of 

app/build.gradle.kts
:
plugins {
    alias(libs.plugins.android.application)
    alias(libs.plugins.kotlin.compose)
    alias(libs.plugins.kotlin.serialization)
    alias(libs.plugins.ksp)
    alias(libs.plugins.room)
}

android {
    namespace = "com.yourname.quicknotes"
    compileSdk = 36

    defaultConfig {
        applicationId = "com.yourname.quicknotes"
        minSdk = 24
        targetSdk = 36
        versionCode = 1
        versionName = "1.0.0"
        testInstrumentationRunner = "androidx.test.runner.AndroidJUnitRunner"
    }

    buildTypes {
        release {
            isMinifyEnabled = true
            isShrinkResources = true
            proguardFiles(
                getDefaultProguardFile("proguard-android-optimize.txt"),
                "proguard-rules.pro"
            )
        }
    }

    buildFeatures {
        compose = true
    }
}

room {
    schemaDirectory("$projectDir/schemas")
}

dependencies {
    val composeBom = platform(libs.androidx.compose.bom)
    implementation(composeBom)
    androidTestImplementation(composeBom)

    implementation(libs.androidx.activity.compose)
    implementation(libs.androidx.compose.ui)
    implementation(libs.androidx.compose.ui.tooling.preview)
    implementation(libs.androidx.compose.material3)
    implementation(libs.androidx.compose.material.icons.core)
    implementation(libs.androidx.lifecycle.viewmodel.compose)
    implementation(libs.androidx.lifecycle.runtime.compose)
    implementation(libs.androidx.navigation3.runtime)
    implementation(libs.androidx.navigation3.ui)
    implementation(libs.androidx.room.runtime)
    implementation(libs.androidx.room.ktx)
    implementation(libs.kotlinx.serialization.core)
    ksp(libs.androidx.room.compiler)

    testImplementation(libs.junit)
    androidTestImplementation(libs.androidx.junit)
    androidTestImplementation(libs.androidx.compose.ui.test.junit4)
    debugImplementation(libs.androidx.compose.ui.tooling)
    debugImplementation(libs.androidx.compose.ui.test.manifest)
}

This is the most important configuration file in the project, so read it carefully.

The 

namespace
is the package used for the generated 
R
class, while 
applicationId
is the identity of the app on devices and on Google Play. They usually match.

compileSdk
is the API level your code is compiled against, and 
targetSdk
tells Android which platform behaviors your app has been tested with. When you raise 
targetSdk
, newer behaviors such as enforced edge-to-edge drawing switch on.

versionCode
is an integer that must increase with every upload to Play, while 
versionName
is the human-readable string users see.

The 

release
block turns on R8, which shrinks, obfuscates, and optimizes your code, and 
isShrinkResources
removes unused resources.

The 

room
block tells the Room plugin where to write JSON snapshots of your database schema, which you'll need later when you write migrations.

In the dependencies, 

platform(libs.androidx.compose.bom)
applies the BOM so the Compose libraries line up, and 
ksp(...)
runs the Room compiler at build time. The 
debugImplementation
lines include Compose preview tooling and a test manifest only in debug builds, so they never ship to users.

Click Sync Now in the banner at the top of the editor. If the sync succeeds, you're ready to write code.

How Jetpack Compose Thinks About UI

Before writing screens, it helps to understand the model Compose is built on, because it's different from the older View system.

In Compose, UI is a function of state. You write functions annotated with 

@Composable
that describe what the screen should look like for the current data. You never reach into a view and call 
setText
on it. Instead, when the data changes, Compose calls your function again with the new data and updates only the parts of the screen that actually changed. This re-running is called recomposition.

Here's the smallest useful example:

@Composable
fun Counter() {
    var count by remember { mutableIntStateOf(0) }

    Button(onClick = { count++ }) {
        Text("Clicked $count times")
    }
}

The 

Counter
function declares a piece of state with 
mutableIntStateOf(0)
. Compose watches every read of that state. When the button's 
onClick
lambda increments 
count
, Compose knows that 
Counter
read the old value, so it schedules 
Counter
to run again, and the 
Text
shows the new number.

The 

remember
call is what keeps the value alive across recompositions. Without it, 
count
would reset to zero every time the function ran.

The 

by
keyword is Kotlin property delegation, which lets you read and write 
count
like a regular variable instead of writing 
count.value
.

remember
survives recomposition but not configuration changes such as rotating the phone, because Android destroys and recreates the activity in that case. For simple values that must survive rotation, use 
rememberSaveable
instead. For anything more substantial, such as data loaded from a database, keep the state in a ViewModel, which outlives the activity. You'll use both in this app.

The other core idea is state hoisting. A composable that owns its own state is hard to reuse and hard to test. A better pattern is to pass state in as parameters and pass events out as lambdas, so the composable only displays what it's given and reports what the user did. The caller decides where the state lives. You'll see this pattern in the list screen, where it makes testing straightforward.

How to Structure the App

Create the following packages under 

com.yourname.quicknotes
by right-clicking the package in the Project panel and choosing New > Package:
com.yourname.quicknotes
├── data/
│   ├── Note.kt
│   ├── NoteDao.kt
│   ├── NotesDatabase.kt
│   └── NoteRepository.kt
├── ui/
│   ├── NotesViewModel.kt
│   ├── NoteListScreen.kt
│   ├── NoteEditorScreen.kt
│   └── theme/
├── navigation/
│   └── NavKeys.kt
├── MainActivity.kt
└── NotesApp.kt

The layout groups files by layer.

The 

data
package holds everything related to storage: the 
Note
entity, the DAO (data access object) that defines queries, the Room database class, and a repository that the rest of the app uses instead of talking to Room directly.

The 

ui
package contains the ViewModel and the two screens, plus the theme files the template generated.

The 

navigation
package holds the keys that identify each screen. 
MainActivity
is the single activity that hosts all of the Compose UI, and 
NotesApp
is a custom 
Application
class used to create the database once for the whole app.

For a larger app, you would likely split these into separate Gradle modules, but packages are enough here.

How to Store Data Locally with Room

Room is the Jetpack persistence library. You describe tables as Kotlin classes and queries as annotated interface methods, and Room generates the SQLite code at compile time. Because queries are checked during the build, a typo in a column name becomes a compiler error instead of a crash on a user's phone.

Start with the entity in 

data/Note.kt
:
package com.yourname.quicknotes.data

import androidx.room.Entity
import androidx.room.PrimaryKey

@Entity(tableName = "notes")
data class Note(
    @PrimaryKey(autoGenerate = true) val id: Long = 0,
    val title: String,
    val body: String,
    val updatedAt: Long = System.currentTimeMillis()
)


@Entity
tells Room that this class maps to a table named 
notes
, and each property becomes a column.

The 

id
field is the primary key, and 
autoGenerate = true
asks SQLite to assign a new ID when you insert a row whose ID is 
0
. That's why 
id
defaults to 
0
: a new note doesn't have a real ID until it's saved.

The 

updatedAt
property stores a timestamp in milliseconds and defaults to the current time whenever a 
Note
object is created, which is how the app knows which notes were edited most recently.

Using a plain 

data class
gives you 
equals
, 
hashCode
, and 
copy
for free, which Compose relies on to decide whether a list item has changed.

Next, define the queries in 

data/NoteDao.kt
:
package com.yourname.quicknotes.data

import androidx.room.Dao
import androidx.room.Delete
import androidx.room.Query
import androidx.room.Upsert
import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.Flow

@Dao
interface NoteDao {
    @Query("SELECT * FROM notes ORDER BY updatedAt DESC")
    fun observeAll(): Flow>

    @Query("SELECT * FROM notes WHERE id = :id")
    suspend fun getById(id: Long): Note?

    @Upsert
    suspend fun upsert(note: Note)

    @Delete
    suspend fun delete(note: Note)
}

A DAO is an interface whose implementation Room writes for you. The 

observeAll
method returns a 
Flow>
rather than a plain list. A 
Flow
is a stream from Kotlin coroutines that emits a new value whenever the underlying data changes, so any time a note is inserted, updated, or deleted, Room automatically re-runs the query and emits the fresh list. This is what keeps the list screen in sync without any manual refresh logic.

The other methods are marked 

suspend
, which means they must be called from a coroutine. Room runs them on a background thread, so database work never blocks the main thread and freezes the UI.

@Upsert
inserts a row if its primary key doesn't exist and updates it if it does, which lets one method handle both creating and editing a note.

The 

:id
syntax in the second query binds the method parameter to the SQL statement safely, with no string concatenation.

Now create the database in 

data/NotesDatabase.kt
:
package com.yourname.quicknotes.data

import androidx.room.Database
import androidx.room.RoomDatabase

@Database(entities = [Note::class], version = 1, exportSchema = true)
abstract class NotesDatabase : RoomDatabase() {
    abstract fun noteDao(): NoteDao
}

The 

@Database
annotation lists every entity in the database and a schema version number. Room generates a concrete subclass of this abstract class, including the implementation of 
noteDao()
.

The 

version
field matters once your app is live. If you later add a column to 
Note
, you must bump the version and provide a migration, or Room will refuse to open the existing database on users' devices.

exportSchema = true
writes a JSON description of each schema version to the 
schemas
folder you configured in Gradle. Commit that folder to version control, because Room uses those files to verify and auto-generate migrations.

How to Expose Data with a Repository and Application Class

The repository is a thin layer between the ViewModel and Room. In this app it mostly forwards calls, but it gives you one place to add caching, network sync, or validation later without touching the UI code. Create 

data/NoteRepository.kt
:
package com.yourname.quicknotes.data

import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.Flow

class NoteRepository(private val noteDao: NoteDao) {

    fun observeNotes(): Flow> = noteDao.observeAll()

    suspend fun getNote(id: Long): Note? = noteDao.getById(id)

    suspend fun save(note: Note) = noteDao.upsert(note)

    suspend fun delete(note: Note) = noteDao.delete(note)
}

The repository takes a 

NoteDao
in its constructor instead of creating one itself. This is dependency injection in its simplest form. Because the dependency is passed in, a test could hand the repository a fake DAO. The public methods use domain language (
save
, 
observeNotes
) rather than database language (
upsert
, 
observeAll
), which keeps Room details from leaking into the rest of the app.

The database should be created exactly once per app process, because opening SQLite is expensive and multiple instances can conflict. A common way to do that without a dependency injection framework is a custom 

Application
subclass. Create 
NotesApp.kt
in the root package:
package com.yourname.quicknotes

import android.app.Application
import androidx.room.Room
import com.yourname.quicknotes.data.NoteRepository
import com.yourname.quicknotes.data.NotesDatabase

class NotesApp : Application() {

    private val database: NotesDatabase by lazy {
        Room.databaseBuilder(this, NotesDatabase::class.java, "notes.db").build()
    }

    val repository: NoteRepository by lazy {
        NoteRepository(database.noteDao())
    }
}

Android creates one instance of the 

Application
class before any activity starts, and keeps it for the lifetime of the process. That makes it a natural home for app-wide singletons.

The 

by lazy
delegate defers creating the database until the first time 
repository
is accessed, which keeps app startup fast.

Room.databaseBuilder
takes a context, the database class, and a file name, and 
build()
returns the generated implementation. For larger apps, Hilt or Koin can manage this wiring for you, but the manual approach shows exactly what those frameworks automate.

For Android to use this class, register it in 

AndroidManifest.xml
by adding the 
android:name
attribute to the
tag:

The only line you're adding is 

android:name=".NotesApp"
. The leading dot is shorthand for your app's namespace, so Android resolves it to 
com.yourname.quicknotes.NotesApp
.

The other attributes came from the template: the launcher icon, the app label shown under the icon, right-to-left layout support, and the base theme used before Compose draws its first frame. If you forget the 

android:name
attribute, Android uses the default 
Application
class and your app crashes the first time it tries to cast it to 
NotesApp
.

How to Manage UI State with a ViewModel

A 

ViewModel
holds the state for a screen and survives configuration changes. When the user rotates the phone, the activity is destroyed and recreated, but the ViewModel stays in memory, so the list of notes doesn't need to be reloaded. Create 
ui/NotesViewModel.kt
:
package com.yourname.quicknotes.ui

import androidx.lifecycle.ViewModel
import androidx.lifecycle.ViewModelProvider
import androidx.lifecycle.viewModelScope
import androidx.lifecycle.viewmodel.initializer
import androidx.lifecycle.viewmodel.viewModelFactory
import com.yourname.quicknotes.NotesApp
import com.yourname.quicknotes.data.Note
import com.yourname.quicknotes.data.NoteRepository
import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.SharingStarted
import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.StateFlow
import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.stateIn
import kotlinx.coroutines.launch

class NotesViewModel(private val repository: NoteRepository) : ViewModel() {

    val notes: StateFlow> = repository.observeNotes()
        .stateIn(
            scope = viewModelScope,
            started = SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000),
            initialValue = emptyList()
        )

    suspend fun getNote(id: Long): Note? = repository.getNote(id)

    fun saveNote(id: Long?, title: String, body: String) {
        viewModelScope.launch {
            repository.save(Note(id = id ?: 0, title = title.trim(), body = body.trim()))
        }
    }

    fun deleteNote(note: Note) {
        viewModelScope.launch {
            repository.delete(note)
        }
    }

    companion object {
        val Factory: ViewModelProvider.Factory = viewModelFactory {
            initializer {
                val app = this[ViewModelProvider.AndroidViewModelFactory.APPLICATION_KEY] as NotesApp
                NotesViewModel(app.repository)
            }
        }
    }
}

There are three ideas packed into this class.

The first is the 

notes
property. 
repository.observeNotes()
returns a cold 
Flow
, which only does work while someone is collecting it. The 
stateIn
operator converts it into a 
StateFlow
, which always holds a current value (starting with an empty list) that the UI can read immediately. 
SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000)
keeps the database query active while the UI is observing and for five seconds after it stops. That five second grace period means a quick rotation doesn't tear down and restart the query, while backgrounding the app for longer does release it.

The second idea is 

viewModelScope
. Saving and deleting are 
suspend
functions, so they need a coroutine. 
viewModelScope
is a coroutine scope tied to the ViewModel's lifetime, and any work launched in it is cancelled automatically when the ViewModel is cleared.

In 

saveNote
, a 
null
ID means "this is a new note," so it becomes 
0
and Room generates a fresh ID. A non-null ID updates the existing row. Because a new 
Note
object is created on every save, 
updatedAt
is refreshed to the current time.

The third idea is the 

Factory
. Android creates ViewModels for you so it can keep them alive across rotations, which means you can't call the constructor directly.

A factory tells Android how to build the ViewModel when it needs one. The 

viewModelFactory
and 
initializer
builders read the 
Application
instance out of the creation extras, cast it to 
NotesApp
, and pass its repository into the constructor.

private fun NoteCard(note: Note, onClick: () -> Unit, onDelete: () -> Unit) {

            verticalAlignment = Alignment.CenterVertically

                        style = MaterialTheme.typography.bodyMedium,

                        overflow = TextOverflow.Ellipsis

NoteListScreen
is the only part that knows about the ViewModel. It calls 
collectAsStateWithLifecycle()
, which turns the 
StateFlow
into Compose state and, unlike the plain 
collectAsState()
, stops collecting when the app moves to the background. That saves battery and avoids doing database work for a screen nobody can see. It then passes the plain list and some lambdas into 
NoteListContent
.

The 

viewModel::deleteNote
syntax is a function reference, a compact way of writing 
{ note -> viewModel.deleteNote(note) }
.

NoteListContent
is stateless. It receives everything as parameters and reports clicks through lambdas, which is state hoisting in practice. Inside it, 
Scaffold
is a Material 3 layout that provides slots for a top app bar and a floating action button and calculates 
innerPadding
so your content doesn't end up behind those bars or behind the system status and navigation bars.

When the list is empty, the screen shows a centered message. Otherwise it uses 

LazyColumn
, which only composes the rows that are currently visible, like 
RecyclerView
in the old View system.

The 

key = { it.id }
argument gives each row a stable identity, so when a note is deleted Compose knows exactly which row to remove instead of redrawing everything below it.

NoteCard
draws one note. 
Modifier
chains configure layout and behavior in order: 
fillMaxWidth()
stretches the card across the screen and 
clickable
makes the whole card respond to taps.

Inside the 

Row
, 
Modifier.weight(1f)
tells the text column to take all horizontal space left over after the delete button is measured. The 
contentDescription
values on icons are read aloud by TalkBack, Android's screen reader. Including the note title in the delete button's description means a TalkBack user hears "Delete Groceries" instead of a row of identical "Delete" buttons.

fun NoteEditorScreen(

                    TextButton(
                            viewModel.saveNote(noteId, title, body)
                            onDone()
                        },
                        enabled = title.isNotBlank()
                    ) {
                        Text("Save")
                    }
                }
            )
        }
    ) { innerPadding ->
        Column(
            modifier = Modifier
                .fillMaxSize()
                .padding(innerPadding)
                .imePadding()
                .padding(16.dp)
        ) {
            OutlinedTextField(
                value = title, title = it },
                label = { Text("Title") },
                singleLine = true,
                modifier = Modifier.fillMaxWidth()
            )
            Spacer(Modifier.height(12.dp))

The editor keeps the text the user is typing in local state with 

rememberSaveable
, so a half-written note survives a rotation. The 
loaded
flag tracks whether the existing note has already been read from the database. It starts as 
true
for new notes (nothing to load) and 
false
for existing ones.

LaunchedEffect(noteId)
runs a coroutine when the composable first appears and again only if 
noteId
changes. Inside it, the screen asks the ViewModel for the note and copies its title and body into the text fields.

Checking 

loaded
before loading is important. Without that check, rotating the screen would run the effect again and overwrite whatever the user had typed with the saved version from the database.

OutlinedTextField
is a Material 3 text input. Compose text fields are controlled components: the field shows whatever 
value
you pass in, and when the user types, it calls 
onValueChange
with the new text. If you forget to update 
title
in that callback, the field appears frozen because Compose keeps redrawing the old value. The Save button is disabled while the title is blank, and pressing it saves through the ViewModel and calls 
onDone
to go back.

imePadding()
adds space at the bottom equal to the height of the on-screen keyboard, so the body field shrinks instead of hiding behind the keyboard. The back arrow uses the 
AutoMirrored
icon set, which flips automatically in right-to-left languages such as Arabic and Hebrew.

How to Add Navigation with Navigation 3

Navigation 3 is the Compose-first navigation library from the Jetpack team. The earlier Navigation Compose library was adapted from a system designed for fragments and treated the back stack as something it owned internally.

Navigation 3 takes the opposite approach: the back stack is a plain list that you own, and navigating means adding or removing items from that list. The library observes the list and shows the screen for whatever key is on top.

First, define a key for each screen in 

navigation/NavKeys.kt
:
package com.yourname.quicknotes.navigation

import androidx.navigation3.runtime.NavKey
import kotlinx.serialization.Serializable

@Serializable
data object NoteList : NavKey

@Serializable
data class NoteEditor(val noteId: Long? = null) : NavKey

Each destination is a type that implements 

NavKey
. 
NoteList
takes no arguments, so it's a 
data object
, a singleton with a readable 
toString
.

NoteEditor
carries an optional note ID, where 
null
means "create a new note." Arguments are typed properties instead of strings embedded in a URL route, so the compiler catches mistakes such as passing the wrong type.

The 

@Serializable
annotation lets Navigation 3 save the back stack when Android kills your app in the background and restore it when the user comes back, which is why the serialization plugin was added earlier.

Now replace 

MainActivity.kt
with the following:
package com.yourname.quicknotes

import android.os.Bundle
import androidx.activity.ComponentActivity
import androidx.activity.compose.setContent
import androidx.activity.enableEdgeToEdge
import androidx.compose.runtime.Composable
import androidx.lifecycle.viewmodel.compose.viewModel
import androidx.navigation3.runtime.entryProvider
import androidx.navigation3.runtime.rememberNavBackStack
import androidx.navigation3.ui.NavDisplay
import com.yourname.quicknotes.navigation.NoteEditor
import com.yourname.quicknotes.navigation.NoteList
import com.yourname.quicknotes.ui.NoteEditorScreen
import com.yourname.quicknotes.ui.NoteListScreen
import com.yourname.quicknotes.ui.NotesViewModel
import com.yourname.quicknotes.ui.theme.QuickNotesTheme

class MainActivity : ComponentActivity() {
    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
        enableEdgeToEdge()
        setContent {
            QuickNotesTheme {
                QuickNotesNavHost()
            }
        }
    }
}

@Composable
fun QuickNotesNavHost() {
    val backStack = rememberNavBackStack(NoteList)
    val notesViewModel: NotesViewModel = viewModel(factory = NotesViewModel.Factory)

    NavDisplay(
        backStack = backStack, backStack.removeLastOrNull() },
        entryProvider = entryProvider {
            entry {
                NoteListScreen(
                    viewModel = notesViewModel, backStack.add(NoteEditor()) }, id -> backStack.add(NoteEditor(id)) }
                )
            }
            entry { key ->
                NoteEditorScreen(
                    noteId = key.noteId,
                    viewModel = notesViewModel, backStack.removeLastOrNull() }
                )
            }
        }
    )
}


MainActivity
is now just a host. 
enableEdgeToEdge()
lets the app draw behind the status bar and navigation bar (more on that in the next section), and 
setContent
replaces the traditional XML layout with a Compose tree wrapped in the theme the template generated.

QuickNotesNavHost
is where navigation happens. 
rememberNavBackStack(NoteList)
creates a saveable back stack that starts with the list screen. The ViewModel is created once with the factory you wrote earlier and shared by both screens, since they work with the same notes.

NavDisplay
renders the entry for the key at the top of the stack. The 
entryProvider
block maps each key type to its composable with 
entry
. For 
NoteEditor
, the lambda receives the key instance, so 
key.noteId
gives you the typed argument directly.

Navigating forward is 

backStack.add(...)
and going back is 
backStack.removeLastOrNull()
. That's the whole API for basic navigation.

onBack
is called when the user presses the system back button or makes the back gesture, and it removes the top entry. Navigation 3 also supports predictive back, the animation where the previous screen peeks in as the user swipes, without any extra code from you.

Run the app now. You should be able to add notes, see them appear in the list, tap one to edit it, delete notes, rotate the device without losing anything, and close and reopen the app with all notes still there.

How to Handle Theming and Edge-to-Edge Display

The template created a 

ui/theme
package with 
Color.kt
, 
Type.kt
, and 
Theme.kt
. The theme function looks roughly like this:
@Composable
fun QuickNotesTheme(
    darkTheme: Boolean = isSystemInDarkTheme(),
    dynamicColor: Boolean = true,
    content: @Composable () -> Unit
) {
    val colorScheme = when {
        dynamicColor && Build.VERSION.SDK_INT >= Build.VERSION_CODES.S -> {
            val context = LocalContext.current
            if (darkTheme) dynamicDarkColorScheme(context) else dynamicLightColorScheme(context)
        }
        darkTheme -> DarkColorScheme
        else -> LightColorScheme
    }

    MaterialTheme(
        colorScheme = colorScheme,
        typography = Typography,
        content = content
    )
}


MaterialTheme
provides colors and typography to every Material 3 component below it, which is why calls such as 
MaterialTheme.typography.titleMedium
in your screens work.

The 

when
block picks a color scheme. On Android 12 (API 31, 
VERSION_CODES.S
) and newer, dynamic color generates a palette from the user's wallpaper so your app matches the rest of their phone. On older versions, or if you set 
dynamicColor
to 
false
, it falls back to the fixed 
LightColorScheme
and 
DarkColorScheme
defined in 
Color.kt
. 
isSystemInDarkTheme()
follows the system dark mode setting.

If you want a consistent brand color everywhere, set 

dynamicColor = false
and edit the colors in 
Color.kt
. The Material Theme Builder can generate a full light and dark scheme from a single seed color.

Edge-to-edge means your app draws behind the system bars instead of inside a box between them. Apps that target Android 15 or higher are edge-to-edge by default, and starting with Android 16 the opt-out is gone.

The 

enableEdgeToEdge()
call in 
MainActivity
makes the behavior consistent on older Android versions too and sets the system bar icons to the correct light or dark color. Because both screens use 
Scaffold
and apply its 
innerPadding
, the content already avoids the bars.

When you build screens without 

Scaffold
, use modifiers such as 
Modifier.safeDrawingPadding()
or 
Modifier.systemBarsPadding()
to keep text and buttons out from under the status bar and gesture area.

How to Prepare the App for Release

A debug build is fine for development, but there are several things to take care of before anyone else installs your app.

Replace the Default App Icon

The template ships with the generic green Android icon. Right-click the 

res
folder and choose New > Image Asset. Image Asset Studio generates an adaptive icon, which has a separate foreground and background layer so launchers can mask it into circles, squircles, or other shapes.

Keep the important part of your artwork inside the central safe zone shown in the preview, because the edges get cropped on some launchers. Also provide a monochrome layer. Android 13 and newer use it for themed icons, where the launcher tints every icon to match the wallpaper, and an app without one looks out of place on those phones.

Move Hardcoded Strings into Resources

The screens in this article use hardcoded strings like 

"Quick Notes"
and 
"No notes yet"
to keep the code readable. In a real app, you'd want to move them into 
res/values/strings.xml
and read them with 
stringResource(R.string.no_notes)
.

That is what makes translation possible, since Android picks the right 

strings.xml
for the user's language automatically. Android Studio flags hardcoded strings with a lint warning and can extract them for you with the Extract string resource quick fix.

Check the Release Build with R8

You enabled 

isMinifyEnabled
in the release build type, which turns on R8. R8 removes unused code, shortens class and method names, and optimizes what remains. That typically makes an app noticeably smaller and faster, but it can break code that relies on reflection, because R8 can't see that a class is used if nothing references it directly.

Room, Compose, and kotlinx.serialization ship their own keep rules, so this app needs no extra configuration. If you add libraries that use reflection, check their documentation for rules to add to 

proguard-rules.pro
.

The way to catch R8 problems is to actually run a release build before uploading it. Select the 

release
variant from Build > Select Build Variant (it will use a debug signing key until you set up release signing in the next section), install it, and click through every screen. A crash that only appears in release builds is almost always a missing keep rule.

Remove Unnecessary Permissions

Open your merged manifest (the Merged Manifest tab at the bottom of 

AndroidManifest.xml
) and look at the permissions listed. Libraries can add permissions you never asked for, and every permission you declare has to be justified in Play Console declarations. Quick Notes stores everything locally, so it shouldn't need any permissions at all, not even 
INTERNET
. Fewer permissions also make the Data safety form in Play Console simpler to fill out.

How to Create an Upload Key and Sign Your App

Every Android app must be cryptographically signed before it can be installed. Google Play uses a two-key system called Play App Signing. You sign your uploads with an upload key that you create and keep. Google verifies the upload, strips your signature, and re-signs the app with an app signing key that Google stores in its own secure infrastructure. Users only ever see the app signing key.

The benefit of this split is recovery. If you lose your upload key or it leaks, you can ask Google to reset it from Play Console, and your users keep receiving updates. Before Play App Signing existed, losing your only signing key meant you could never update your app again.

Play App Signing is mandatory for new apps, and it's also what makes Android App Bundles possible, since Google needs the signing key to generate optimized APKs for each device.

Create an upload key from the terminal with 

keytool
, which comes with the JDK bundled in Android Studio:
keytool -genkeypair -v \
  -keystore ~/keys/quicknotes-upload.jks \
  -alias upload \
  -keyalg RSA -keysize 2048 \
  -validity 10000

This command creates a Java keystore file at 

~/keys/quicknotes-upload.jks
containing one key pair with the alias 
upload
. 
-keyalg RSA -keysize 2048
sets the key type and strength Google Play expects, and 
-validity 10000
makes the key valid for roughly 27 years. Google Play requires keys to be valid until at least October 2033.

The tool prompts for a keystore password and asks for your name and organization, which are stored in the certificate. If 

keytool
isn't on your path, Android Studio's Build > Generate Signed App Bundle or APK wizard can create the same key through a dialog.

Store the keystore somewhere outside your project folder and back it up to a password manager or encrypted storage. Never commit it to Git.

Next, create a 

keystore.properties
file in your project root to hold the signing details:
storeFile=/Users/yourname/keys/quicknotes-upload.jks
storePassword=your-keystore-password
keyAlias=upload
keyPassword=your-key-password

This file maps the four values Gradle needs to sign a build: the path to the keystore, the keystore password, the alias of the key inside it, and the password for that key. Keeping them in a separate file lets you share the project without sharing secrets. Add 

keystore.properties
and 
*.jks
to your 
.gitignore
right away.

Then load the file in 

app/build.gradle.kts
and create a release signing configuration:
import java.util.Properties

val keystorePropertiesFile = rootProject.file("keystore.properties")
val keystoreProperties = Properties().apply {
    if (keystorePropertiesFile.exists()) {
        keystorePropertiesFile.inputStream().use { load(it) }
    }
}

android {
    // namespace, compileSdk, defaultConfig as before

    signingConfigs {
        if (keystorePropertiesFile.exists()) {
            create("release") {
                storeFile = file(keystoreProperties.getProperty("storeFile"))
                storePassword = keystoreProperties.getProperty("storePassword")
                keyAlias = keystoreProperties.getProperty("keyAlias")
                keyPassword = keystoreProperties.getProperty("keyPassword")
            }
        }
    }

    buildTypes {
        release {
            isMinifyEnabled = true
            isShrinkResources = true
            proguardFiles(
                getDefaultProguardFile("proguard-android-optimize.txt"),
                "proguard-rules.pro"
            )
            signingConfig = signingConfigs.findByName("release")
        }
    }
}

The 

import
must go at the very top of the file, above the 
plugins
block. The script reads 
keystore.properties
into a 
Properties
object if the file exists.

Inside 

signingConfigs
, it creates a configuration named 
release
from those values, but only when the file is present. That guard matters because a teammate cloning the repository, or a CI server running tests, won't have your keystore, and the build should still work for debug tasks.

The release build type then uses 

findByName("release")
, which returns 
null
instead of failing when the config doesn't exist. In a CI pipeline, you would typically read these values from environment variables or a secrets manager instead of a file.

How to Build an Android App Bundle

Google Play doesn't accept APKs for new apps. You upload an Android App Bundle (AAB) instead. A bundle contains all of your compiled code and resources for every screen density, CPU architecture, and language. When a user installs the app, Google Play generates an APK containing only what that specific device needs. A phone with an English locale and a high density screen doesn't download Japanese strings or low density images, so the download is smaller.

Build the bundle from the terminal:

./gradlew bundleRelease

This task compiles the release variant, runs R8, signs the result with your upload key, and writes the bundle to 

app/build/outputs/bundle/release/app-release.aab
. You can also use Build > Generate Signed App Bundle or APK in Android Studio, which does the same thing through a wizard. If the build fails with a signing error, double-check the path and passwords in 
keystore.properties
.

Before uploading, increase 

versionCode
for every new build you send to Play. The first upload can use 
1
, the next must be 
2
or higher, and so on. Play rejects any bundle whose 
versionCode
it has already seen, even on a different testing track. 
versionName
can be anything, but semantic versions such as 
1.0.0
, 
1.0.1
, and 
1.1.0
are easy for users and for you to follow.

How to Create a Google Play Developer Account

Go to play.google.com/console and sign in with the Google account you want to own the developer account. Consider creating a dedicated account for this rather than using your personal Gmail, since transferring ownership later is awkward.

You'll be asked to choose between a personal account and an organization account. A personal account is for individuals. An organization account is for registered businesses and requires a D-U-N-S number, a free business identifier from Dun and Bradstreet that can take a week or more to obtain.

The choice affects more than paperwork. New personal accounts must complete a closed testing period before they can publish to production (covered below), while organization accounts are exempt from that requirement. Your developer name and, for organizations and monetized personal accounts, your address are shown publicly on your store listing.

Pay the one-time 25 USD registration fee, then complete identity verification. Google asks for a legal name and address matching a government ID, verifies your contact email and phone number, and for personal accounts asks you to confirm that you have access to a physical Android device by installing the Play Console app and signing in. Verification usually takes a few days. You can't publish until it's complete, so start this step early, even before your app is finished.

Identity verification is becoming more important across the Android ecosystem. Google has begun rolling out developer verification for all apps installed on certified Android devices, including those distributed outside Google Play, starting with a handful of countries in late 2026. If you distribute through Play and have completed Play Console verification, you're already covered, but it's one more reason to make sure your account details are accurate.

How to Create Your App in the Play Console

Once your account is verified, click Create app on the Play Console home page. Enter the app name as it should appear on Google Play (up to 30 characters), select the default language, choose App rather than Game, and choose Free or Paid.

Be careful here. You can change a paid app to free later, but a free app can never become paid. If you want to charge money, use in-app purchases or subscriptions instead. Accept the Developer Program Policies and US export law declarations and click Create app.

You land on the app dashboard, which shows a checklist of tasks grouped into sections. Play Console walks you through them in a sensible order, but the next two sections cover the parts that confuse people most.

How to Complete the App Content Declarations

Under Policy and programs > App content (also linked from the dashboard checklist), Google asks a series of questions about your app. Every app must complete all of them before it can be released to any track, including internal testing.

The Privacy policy requires a public URL to a page describing what data your app collects and how it's used. This is required even if your app collects nothing. For Quick Notes, a short page stating that notes are stored only on the device and no data is collected or shared is enough. You can host it with GitHub Pages, Google Sites, or your own website, but it must be a working public web page, not a PDF or a Google Doc that requires sign-in.

App access asks whether parts of the app require login. If they do, you must provide test credentials so reviewers can reach every screen. Quick Notes has no login, so select that all functionality is available without special access.

Ads asks whether your app contains ads, including ads from SDKs you didn't write yourself. Answer honestly, because apps with ads get a "Contains ads" label on the store listing and reviewers check.

Content rating is an IARC questionnaire about violence, sexual content, language, controlled substances, user interaction, and similar topics. Your answers produce age ratings for regions around the world (ESRB in North America, PEGI in Europe, and so on). A notes app with no user-generated sharing will receive the lowest rating everywhere.

Target audience and content asks which age groups your app is designed for. If you include children under 13, your app falls under the Families policy, which adds requirements around ads, data collection, and SDKs. For a general purpose utility, choose 18 and over or a range starting at 13, unless children really are your audience.

Data safety is the most detailed form. It produces the "Data safety" section on your store listing and asks whether your app collects or shares each type of user data, such as location, contacts, personal info, and app activity, and for what purpose. The trap is that you're responsible for data collected by every library in your app, not only your own code. Analytics, crash reporting, and ad SDKs all collect data and must be declared.

Most major SDKs publish a page explaining exactly what to declare. Quick Notes uses no such libraries and makes no network calls, so the honest answer is that no data is collected or shared.

The remaining declarations (news apps, government apps, financial features, health apps, and others) are yes or no questions. For a notes app, the answer to each is no.

How to Set Up Your Store Listing

The store listing, under Grow users > Store presence > Main store listing, is what people see before they install. It needs the following text and graphics.

AssetRequirement
App nameUp to 30 characters
Short descriptionUp to 80 characters
Full descriptionUp to 4000 characters
App icon512 x 512 px PNG, 32-bit with alpha, up to 1 MB
Feature graphic1024 x 500 px JPEG or 24-bit PNG, no alpha
Phone screenshots2 to 8 images, 16:9 or 9:16, each side between 320 and 3840 px

The left column lists each required asset and the right column lists Google's current limits.

The short description appears directly under your app name in search results, so treat it as your one-line pitch and put your most important keyword in it. The full description is where you explain features in plain language. Google Play indexes it for search, but stuffing it with keywords violates the metadata policy and can get your listing rejected.

The 512 px icon is separate from the launcher icon inside the app, though it should look the same. Google applies the rounded mask itself, so upload a full square without pre-rounded corners or drop shadows. The feature graphic appears at the top of your listing in some layouts and when your app is promoted.

Screenshots are the biggest factor in whether someone installs. Capture them from the emulator using the camera button in the emulator toolbar, and consider adding short captions that explain what each screen does. If you want your app to show up well on tablets and Chromebooks, Play Console has separate slots for tablet screenshots, and providing them improves your listing on those devices.

Also fill in the Store settings page with an app category (Productivity fits Quick Notes), tags, and a contact email address. The contact email is shown publicly on the listing.

How to Run Internal and Closed Testing

Google Play has several release tracks. Internal testing is for up to 100 testers you add by email, and builds are usually available within minutes with minimal review. Closed testing is for a larger group you control, either by email list or Google Group. Open testing lets anyone join from the store listing. Production is the public release.

Start with internal testing. Go to Test and release > Testing > Internal testing, create an email list of testers (you can include yourself), and click Create new release. The first time, Play Console asks you to confirm Play App Signing. Accept the default, which lets Google generate and protect the app signing key. Then upload your 

app-release.aab
, enter release notes, and roll out the release.

Share the opt-in link from the Testers tab with your testers. They accept the invitation in a browser and can then install the app from Google Play like any other app. Installing through Play, instead of sideloading, proves the bundle works end to end with Play App Signing.

If you created a personal developer account, you can't publish to production right away. Personal accounts created after November 13, 2023 must run a closed test with at least 12 testers who have stayed opted in for the last 14 days continuously. Google introduced this rule to cut down on low-quality and abandoned apps, and it's the step that catches the most first-time developers by surprise.

Set this up under Test and release > Testing > Closed testing. Create a track, add testers through an email list or a Google Group, and upload a release (you can promote the same build from internal testing).

Recruit testers early. Friends, family, coworkers, and developer communities are the usual sources. The 12 testers must actually opt in through the link, and the count is of testers who remain opted in, so if someone leaves on day 10, your clock is affected. Plan for more than 12 to give yourself a buffer.

Use the 14 days productively. Ask testers to send feedback, watch for crashes in Monitor and improve > Android vitals, and push updated builds as you fix problems. Each update needs a higher 

versionCode
. When Google reviews your production access request, it looks at whether you used the test to improve the app, not only whether time passed.

When the 14 days are up, the dashboard shows an Apply for production button. The application asks how you recruited testers, what feedback you received, what you changed as a result, and whether the app is ready for release. Answer specifically. Vague answers like "testers liked it" are a common reason for rejection. Approval typically takes up to a week.

How to Publish to Production

Once you have production access, go to Test and release > Production and click Create new release. You can upload a new bundle or promote one from a testing track. Add release notes in the "What's new" field. Users see these on the store listing and in the update notification.

Before rolling out, choose which countries and regions to make the app available in, under the Countries / regions tab of the Production page. Then review the release summary. Play Console shows any errors that block the release (such as an incomplete declaration) and warnings that do not (such as missing translations). Fix the errors, read the warnings, and click Send for review.

Every new app and every update goes through review. For a brand new app, the first review can take up to seven days and occasionally longer. Later updates usually take a day or two. If the app is rejected, Play Console and your developer email explain which policy was violated. Fix the issue, increment the 

versionCode
, and resubmit.

By default, approved releases go live as soon as they pass review. If you want to control the launch date, turn on Managed publishing in the Publishing overview page. Approved changes then wait until you click Publish, which is useful when you're coordinating with a blog post or a marketing date.

How to Ship Updates After Launch

Getting your app live is the start of maintenance, not the end of the project. Three habits make updates go smoothly.

The first is staged rollouts. When you release an update to production, Play Console lets you choose a percentage of users to receive it, such as 10 percent. Watch crash and ANR (App Not Responding) rates in Android vitals for a day or two, then increase the percentage. If something goes wrong, you can halt the rollout, and the remaining users never get the broken version.

Google uses Android vitals thresholds to decide whether to show warnings on your listing or reduce its visibility, so catching problems at 10 percent matters.

The second is keeping your target SDK current. Google Play raises the minimum 

targetSdk
for updates every year. If your app falls behind, you can no longer publish updates, and after a grace period new users on recent Android versions may not be able to find it.

Raising 

targetSdk
isn't just changing a number. Read the behavior changes page for each new Android version and test your app against them. A good routine is to install the Android beta on a test device or emulator each spring so the August deadline is never a surprise.

The third is planning for database changes. When you add a column to 

Note
or create a new entity, increment the 
version
in 
@Database
and give Room a migration. For simple changes, such as adding a column with a default value, Room can generate the migration if you declare 
autoMigrations = [AutoMigration(from = 1, to = 2)]
in the annotation, using the schema JSON files you exported. Skipping this step causes a crash for every existing user the moment they open the updated app, and it's one of the most common causes of one-star reviews after an update.

Summary

In this handbook, you built a complete native Android app with the tools Google currently recommends.

Jetpack Compose describes the UI as functions of state, and the state hoisting pattern keeps screens such as 

NoteListContent
simple to test. Room provides compile-time checked storage that streams updates through a 
Flow
, and a ViewModel exposes that data as a 
StateFlow
that survives rotation. Navigation 3 treats the back stack as an ordinary list you own, so navigating forward and back are just 
add
and 
removeLastOrNull
.

On the release side, you configured R8 to shrink the app, created an upload key and stored it safely outside the project, and built a signed Android App Bundle. Play App Signing means Google holds the final signing key, so losing your upload key is recoverable instead of fatal.

Publishing to Google Play takes more than an upload. You verified your developer identity, filled in the privacy policy, content rating, and Data safety declarations honestly (including data collected by third party libraries), built a store listing, and, for a personal account, ran a 14 day closed test with at least 12 testers before applying for production access. Planning for that testing window from the start is the biggest thing you can do to avoid a delayed launch.

From here, good next steps are adding a dependency injection framework such as Hilt as the app grows, syncing notes to a backend, adding a second language through 

strings.xml
, and setting up a CI pipeline that runs your tests and builds a signed bundle on every tagged release. The full flow you followed in this handbook stays the same no matter how large the app becomes.
